lessons.title: Mole and Avogadro's Number
lessons.notes_html:
Stoichiometry is the study of the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a chemical reaction using a balanced chemical equation. The central counting unit of stoichiometry is the mole, which links the mass of a substance with the number of its particles.

The Mole

A mole is the gram atomic mass, gram molecular mass or gram formula mass of a substance, and it contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles (atoms, molecules or ions). For example, one mole of carbon atoms weighs 12g and contains 6.02 x 10^23 atoms, while one mole of water weighs 18g and contains 6.02 x 10^23 molecules.

Avogadro's Number

Avogadro's number is the number of particles present in one mole of any substance, equal to 6.02 x 10^23 and denoted by NA. It is a constant: it does not change with temperature. With its help the mole becomes a counting unit like a dozen: just as one dozen means 12 objects, one mole means 6.02 x 10^23 particles. The mole and Avogadro's number are interrelated because the mole is defined through it: one mole of every substance, whatever its mass in grams, always contains Avogadro's number of particles.

Number of moles = Number of particles / 6.02 x 10^23

Molar Volume

Molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at STP (273K and 1 atm pressure); for all ideal gases its value is 22.4 dm3. So 44.8 dm3 of O2 at STP = 44.8/22.4 = 2 moles = 2 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 12.04 x 10^23 molecules.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Calculate the number of moles and molecules in (i) 38g of carbon disulphide (CS2) (ii) 68.4g of sucrose (C12H22O11). Solution: (i) Molar mass of CS2 = 12 + 2(32) = 76 g/mol. Moles = 38/76 = 0.499 moles (about 0.5 mole). Molecules = 0.499 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 3.0 x 10^23 molecules. (ii) Molar mass of sucrose = 12(12) + 22(1) + 11(16) = 342 g/mol. Moles = 68.4/342 = 0.199 moles (about 0.2 mole). Molecules = 0.199 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.19 x 10^23 molecules.

Numerical 2: 1.6g of a sample of gas occupies a volume of 1.12 dm3 at STP. Determine the molar mass of the substance. Solution: At STP one mole of a gas occupies 22.4 dm3. Moles of gas = 1.12/22.4 = 0.05 mol. Molar mass = mass / moles = 1.6/0.05 = 32 g/mol.

Numerical 3: Calculate (i) number of moles in 6.4g of SO2 (ii) mass in grams of 4.5 moles of ethyne (C2H2) (iii) volume in cm3 of 38.4g O2 gas at STP (iv) number of molecules of 126g water (v) mass in grams of 4.8 x 10^24 atoms of sodium (vi) number of formula units in 333g of CaCl2. Solution: (i) Moles = 6.4/64 = 0.1 mol. (ii) Molar mass of C2H2 = 26 g/mol, mass = 4.5 x 26 = 117g. (iii) Moles of O2 = 38.4/32 = 1.2 mol; volume = 1.2 x 22400 = 26880 cm3 at STP. (iv) Moles of water = 126/18 = 7 mol; molecules = 7 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 42.14 x 10^23. (v) Moles of Na = 4.8 x 10^24 / 6.02 x 10^23 = 7.97 mol; mass = 7.97 x 23 = 183.39g. (vi) Moles of CaCl2 = 333/111 = 3 mol; formula units = 3 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 18.06 x 10^23.

lessons.title: Rounding off Data
lessons.notes_html:
Experimental measurements often give numbers with more digits than are significant. Rounding of data is a method of reducing the figures in a given numerical value to the desired significant figures.

Rules of Rounding off Data

  • Rounding means reducing a number to the desired significant figures and adjusting the last reported digit.
  • If the digit to be dropped is less than 5, the last retained digit stays unchanged.
  • If the digit to be dropped is greater than 5, the last retained digit is increased by one.
  • If the digit to be dropped is exactly 5, the last retained digit is increased by one only if it is odd, and left unchanged if it is even.

lessons.title: Exponential Notation
lessons.notes_html:
Very large and very small numbers in chemistry, such as Avogadro's number, are conveniently written in exponential notation.

Exponential Notation

Exponential notation is a shorthand mathematical form in which a number is written as a coefficient multiplied by 10 raised to some power. The decimal point is moved so that only one non-zero digit is left before it, and the power of 10 counts the places moved.

  • 3652 = 3.652 x 10^3
  • 0.0231 = 2.31 x 10^-2
  • 0.000072 = 7.2 x 10^-5

Converting Back to Simple Numbers

A negative power moves the decimal point to the left and a positive power moves it to the right.

  • 3.26 x 10^-3 = 0.00326
  • 1.921 x 10^2 = 192.1
  • 1.02 x 10^5 = 102000

lessons.title: Limiting Reactant and its Calculations
lessons.notes_html:
In a reaction mixture the reactants are not always present in exactly the amounts required by the balanced equation. The reactant that runs out first controls how much product can form.

Limiting Reactant

The limiting reactant is the reactant which is consumed entirely when a chemical reaction is completed, while the other reactant is left partly unused (reactant in excess). It controls the amount of product because the reaction stops as soon as the limiting reactant is used up, even though the excess reactant is still present. Therefore the quantity of product is always calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant. For example, if hydrogen is limiting in the burning of hydrogen in oxygen, the water formed depends only on the hydrogen available.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Ammonia gas can be produced by heating together solid NH4Cl and Ca(OH)2: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NH3 + CaCl2 + 2H2O. If a mixture containing 100g of each of these solids is heated, determine the limiting reactant and the mass of NH3 gas produced. Solution: Moles of NH4Cl = 100/53.5 = 1.87 mol; moles of Ca(OH)2 = 100/74 = 1.35 mol. The equation needs 2 moles NH4Cl for 1 mole Ca(OH)2, so 1.87 mol NH4Cl needs only 0.935 mol Ca(OH)2, which is available in excess. Hence NH4Cl is the limiting reactant. NH3 formed = 1.87 mol, and mass of NH3 = 1.87 x 17 = 31.7g.

Numerical 2: Silver sulphide (Ag2S) is an anti-microbial agent. In an experiment 24.8g Ag2S is reacted with excess hydrochloric acid: Ag2S(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2AgCl(s) + H2S(g). Calculate (i) the mass of AgCl formed (ii) the volume of H2S produced at STP (atomic mass of Ag = 108 and S = 32). Solution: Molar mass of Ag2S = 2(108) + 32 = 248 g/mol, so moles = 24.8/248 = 0.1 mol. (i) AgCl formed = 2 x 0.1 = 0.2 mol; molar mass of AgCl = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5 g/mol, so mass = 0.2 x 143.5 = 28.7g. (ii) H2S formed = 0.1 mol, so volume at STP = 0.1 x 22.4 = 2.24 dm3.

lessons.title: Theoretical Yield, Practical Yield and Percent Yield
lessons.notes_html:
The amount of product predicted by stoichiometry is rarely the amount actually collected in the laboratory. This lesson defines the three yield terms and how percent yield is calculated.

Theoretical Yield

Theoretical yield is the maximum amount of product calculated from a balanced chemical equation, assuming complete conversion of the limiting reactant.

Actual (Practical) Yield

Actual or practical yield is the amount of product actually obtained during the experiment. Practical yield is often less than theoretical yield because the reaction may not go to completion, side reactions may consume reactants, some product is lost during separation and purification, and the reaction may be reversible.

Percent Yield

Percent yield = (Practical yield / Theoretical yield) x 100

Worked Numerical

Numerical: Aluminum chloride is used in the manufacturing of rubber. It is produced by allowing aluminum to react with Cl2 gas at 650 degree C: 2Al(s) + 3Cl2(g) -> 2AlCl3(l). When 160g aluminum reacts with excess of chlorine, 650g of AlCl3 is produced. What is the percentage yield of AlCl3? Solution: Moles of Al = 160/27 = 5.93 mol, so theoretical moles of AlCl3 = 5.93 mol. Theoretical mass = 5.93 x 133.5 = about 791g. Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100 = (650/791) x 100 = 82.17%.

mcqs.why: Percent yield = (Practical yield / Theoretical yield) x 100, as given in the lesson formula.

lessons.title: Subatomic Particles and their Characteristics
lessons.notes_html:
More than a hundred subatomic particles have been discovered in an atom, such as electron, proton, neutron, positron, mesons and hyperons, however only electron, proton and neutron are considered to be the fundamental particles of an atom which play an important role in the physical and chemical properties of elements. Almost all of the mass of an atom exists in the nucleus, and except protium (isotope of hydrogen), nuclei of all other atoms contain neutrons.

Discovery Timeline

  • Proton was discovered in 1886.
  • Electron was discovered in 1897.
  • Rutherford discovered the nucleus in 1911 and laid the foundation that the atom consists of an extremely charged region called nucleus wherein most of the mass of an atom is concentrated, while electrons revolve in the extra-nuclear part.
  • James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 and was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1935 for this discovery.
  • Millikan, in 1909, performed the oil drop experiment and found that the charge on every oil drop was an integral multiple of 1.6 x 10^-19 Coulomb, which he deduced to be the charge of Thomson's electrons.

Electrons

The electron was discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897 A.D. while studying the cathode rays experiment; he called the cathode rays beam as electrons. Thereafter, Millikan with his oil drop experiment calculated the charge on an electron. Electrons revolve in orbits and occupy about 100,000 times greater volume than the nucleus but form less than one percent total mass of an atom. They carry negative charge whose magnitude is equal to the positive charge of protons, and this attractive force (electrostatic force) keeps electrons constantly moving around the nucleus. The mass of an electron is nearly 1836 times less than a proton and 1839 times less than a neutron. Electronic configuration refers to the presence of electrons in various shells and sub-shells; this arrangement affects atomic stability, melting points, boiling points and density, and electrons are also involved in chemical bond formation.

Protons

Protons are positively charged subatomic particles which are located in the nuclei of all elements. They were discovered by Goldstein (1886 A.D.), a German physicist, by using a perforated cathode in Crook's discharge tube; Rutherford called these positively charged particles "protons". With respect to mass and charge, the protons of all elements are identical to each other. Atomic number of an element is related only to protons, while mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons. About 99.94% mass of an atom exists in the nucleus. Protons and electrons have the same magnitude of charge but have different masses, and all elements have different numbers of protons.

Neutrons

The discovery of the neutron was made by James Chadwick (1932 A.D.) in an artificial radioactivity experiment. He bombarded alpha particles from polonium on beryllium, a stable element, and noted that some highly penetrating neutral particles were produced; these particles were named as neutrons: Be-9 + He-4 -> C-12 + n-1 [neutron]. Like protons, neutrons are also part of the atomic mass, but the neutron has no charge. Neutrons of all elements have the same nature and mass, and they are bound with each other and with protons by nuclear forces.

lessons.title: Bohr's Atomic Theory
lessons.notes_html:
Bohr's theory explains the structure of one-electron species such as H, He+ and Li+2 (it is not applicable to multi-electron species like H-, which has two electrons). Its ideas explain the line spectrum of hydrogen: each element gives a unique line spectrum, so the spectrum acts as a fingerprint for the identification of elements.

Postulates of Bohr's Atomic Theory

  • Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits of definite energy without radiating energy.
  • The angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h/2pi.
  • Energy is absorbed when an electron jumps to a higher orbit and emitted when it falls to a lower orbit, with frequency given by E2 - E1 = hv.

Frequency of the Emitted Radiation

The energy of the electron in orbit n is En = -me^4/(8e0^2 h^2 n^2). For a jump from n2 to n1, the energy emitted is DE = E(n2) - E(n1) = (me^4/8e0^2 h^2)(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2). Since DE = hv, the frequency is v = (me^4/8e0^2 h^3)(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2), which explains the lines of the hydrogen spectrum. The radius of an orbit is given by r = 0.529 x n^2/Z in Angstrom; the radius of the first orbit of hydrogen is 0.529 A.

Hydrogen Spectrum in Terms of Bohr's Theory

In the ground state the electron of hydrogen stays in the first orbit. When energy is supplied, it jumps to higher orbits (n = 2, 3, 4 ...). When it falls back, it emits radiation of fixed frequency, producing a line spectrum. Falls to n = 1 give the Lyman series in the ultraviolet region, falls to n = 2 give the Balmer series in the visible region, and falls to n = 3, 4 and 5 give the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series in the infrared region. Each line corresponds to a definite energy difference between two orbits.

Defects of Bohr's Atomic Model

  • It does not explain the spectra of atoms having more than one electron, such as helium.
  • It cannot explain the fine structure of spectral lines observed under high resolution, nor the splitting of lines in electric and magnetic fields (Stark and Zeeman effects).
  • It treats the electron only as a particle and ignores its wave nature.
  • It violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle by fixing both the position and momentum of the electron.
  • It gives no satisfactory explanation of chemical bonding and molecular formation.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Calculate the radius of hydrogen in the 3rd orbit (Bohr constant for hydrogen is 0.529 A). Solution: rn = 0.529 x n^2/Z. For hydrogen Z = 1 and n = 3, so r3 = 0.529 x 9/1 = 4.761 A. Hence the radius of the third orbit of hydrogen is about 4.76 A.

Numerical 2: A photon of wave number 23 x 10^5 m^-1 is emitted when an electron undergoes a transition from a higher energy orbit to n = 2. Determine the orbit from which the electron falls and the spectral series (Rydberg constant = 1.09678 x 10^7 m^-1). Solution: Wave number = RH (1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2) with n1 = 2. So 23 x 10^5 = 1.09678 x 10^7 (1/4 - 1/n2^2), giving (1/4 - 1/n2^2) = 0.2097. Then 1/n2^2 = 0.25 - 0.2097 = 0.0403, so n2^2 = 24.8 and n2 = about 5. lessons.title: Planck's Quantum Theory
lessons.notes_html:
Planck's quantum theory replaced the idea of continuous energy flow with the idea that energy is emitted or absorbed in small packets. Bohr used this idea when he related the energy difference between orbits to the frequency of radiation: E2 - E1 = hv.

Quanta and Photons

  • Energy is not emitted continuously but in discrete packets called quanta; a quantum of light is called a photon.
  • The energy of one quantum is directly proportional to the frequency of the radiation: E = hv, where h is Planck's constant.
  • This is why each spectral line has a definite frequency: it corresponds to one definite energy difference DE = hv between two orbits.

lessons.title: X-Rays
lessons.notes_html:
X-rays are short wavelength, highly penetrating electromagnetic radiations.

Production of X-Rays

They are produced when fast-moving electrons (cathode rays) strike a metal target of high atomic mass, such as tungsten, in a discharge tube; part of their kinetic energy changes into X-rays.

Properties of X-Rays

  • They travel in straight lines at the speed of light.
  • They are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
  • They penetrate flesh but are stopped by bones and heavy metals.
  • They affect photographic plates.

Uses of X-Rays

  • In medical diagnosis and surgery.
  • In industry for detecting defects in materials.
  • In the study of crystal structure.
  • In the treatment of some diseases.

lessons.title: Quantum Numbers and Orbitals
lessons.notes_html:
In the quantum mechanical picture an electron is not in a fixed orbit but in an orbital, and its state is completely described by four quantum numbers.

The Four Quantum Numbers

  • Principal quantum number (n): describes the size and energy of the shell and takes values 1, 2, 3 ....
  • Azimuthal quantum number (l): describes the shape of the orbital and ranges from 0 to (n - 1). For a 3s orbital, n = 3 and l = 0.
  • Magnetic quantum number (m): describes the orientation of the orbital in space and ranges from -l to +l.
  • Spin quantum number (s): describes the spin of the electron and is +1/2 or -1/2.

For n = 2: l = 0, 1; for l = 0, m = 0; for l = 1, m = -1, 0, +1; and for each electron s = +1/2 or -1/2.

Shapes of Orbitals

  • For l = 0 the orbital is an s orbital, which is spherical in shape, with the electron density distributed equally in all directions around the nucleus.
  • For l = 1 the orbital is a p orbital, which is dumbbell shaped, having two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus separated by a nodal plane. There are three p orbitals (px, py, pz) oriented along the three axes.
  • The size of both types of orbital increases with the principal quantum number n.

Orbit versus Orbital

OrbitOrbital
A well-defined circular path around the nucleus in which an electron revolves, as proposed by BohrA three-dimensional region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is maximum (about 95%)
Position and momentum of the electron can be known at the same timeBased on quantum mechanics and the uncertainty principle
Two-dimensional concept with a fixed radiusHas a definite shape (spherical, dumbbell, etc.) but no fixed path

lessons.title: Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in the shells and sub-shells of an atom. Three rules govern this arrangement.

Pauli's Exclusion Principle

In an atom no two electrons can have the same set of four quantum numbers; at least one quantum number must be different. Hence an orbital can hold at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins, illustrated as one up arrow and one down arrow in the same box.

Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity

When degenerate orbitals are available, electrons fill them singly with the same spin direction so as to give the maximum number of unpaired electrons. For example, nitrogen has the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p1x 2p1y 2p1z and not 1s2 2s2 2p2x 2p1y, because the three p electrons occupy separate p orbitals. This is determined by Hund's rule.

Aufbau Principle and the (n + l) Rule

Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, decided by the (n + l) rule: the orbital with the lower (n + l) value is filled first. This explains why the filling of the 4s orbital takes place prior to 3d: for 4s, (n + l) = 4 + 0 = 4, while for 3d, (n + l) = 3 + 2 = 5, so 4s has lower energy and is filled first. This is why potassium and calcium place their electrons in 4s before 3d begins to fill in the transition metals. After 4d is filled, the next electron enters 5p.

Writing Electronic Configurations

  • Fe (Z = 26): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6
  • Br- (Z = 35) has 35 + 1 = 36 electrons: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6, the same as krypton.
  • Ca+2 (Z = 20) has 20 - 2 = 18 electrons: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6, the same as argon.

Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons: Na+ and Ne, Na+ and F-, and Na+ and Mg+2 are isoelectronic pairs (each has 10 electrons), while Na (11 electrons) and Ca (20 electrons) are not.

lessons.title: Theories of Covalent Bond
lessons.notes_html:
Two theories explain the covalent bond: valence bond theory (VBT), in which the bond is localized between two atoms, and molecular orbital theory (MOT), in which electrons occupy orbitals spread over the whole molecule.

Valence Bond Theory (VBT)

  • A covalent bond is formed by the overlapping of half-filled atomic orbitals of two atoms, and the shared electron pair is localized between the two nuclei.
  • The overlapping takes place in the direction of maximum electron density, and the atoms keep their identity in the molecule.
  • Greater overlapping gives a stronger bond.

Sigma and Pi Bonds

End-to-end (head-on) overlapping along the internuclear axis, such as s-s, s-p and p-p axial overlap, produces a sigma bond, which is strong and allows free rotation. Side-by-side overlapping of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis produces a pi bond, which is weaker and restricts rotation about the bond. A sigma bond is stronger than a pi bond because the overlapping in a sigma bond is head-on and extensive, while in a pi bond the side-by-side overlapping is partial and less effective. In C2H4 there are 5 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond: the four C-H single bonds and one part of the C=C double bond are sigma, and the remaining part of the double bond is pi.

Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)

In MOT, atomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals spread over the whole molecule. A bonding molecular orbital has lower energy than the atomic orbitals and holds the atoms together, while an antibonding molecular orbital has higher energy and tends to separate the atoms.

VBTMOT
Bond formed by overlapping of atomic orbitalsAtomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals
Shared pair stays localized between the two atomsElectrons occupy orbitals spread over the whole molecule

Molecular Orbital Diagram of O2

The molecular orbital diagram of O2 is obtained by combining the atomic orbitals of two oxygen atoms; the 16 electrons fill the molecular orbitals in order of increasing energy.

  • MO configuration: (sigma1s)2 (sigma*1s)2 (sigma2s)2 (sigma*2s)2 (sigma2pz)2 (pi2px)2 (pi2py)2 (pi*2px)1 (pi*2py)1
  • Bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons)/2 = (10 - 6)/2 = 2, so O2 has a double bond. (In N2, bonding electrons are 10 and antibonding 4, so bond order = (10 - 4)/2 = 3, a triple bond.)
  • Paramagnetic behaviour: the two antibonding pi* orbitals each contain one unpaired electron. Because of these two unpaired electrons, O2 is paramagnetic, and this behaviour can only be explained by molecular orbital theory, not by valence bond theory.

lessons.title: Shape of the Molecules
lessons.notes_html:
The shape of a molecule is decided by the repulsion between the electron pairs around its central atom, and by the hybridization of that atom.

VSEPR Theory

  • The shape of a molecule is determined by the repulsion between electron pairs around the central atom.
  • The pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimize repulsion.
  • Repulsion decreases in the order: lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair.

Shapes Predicted by VSEPR Theory

MoleculeBond PairsLone PairsShape
AlCl330Planar trigonal
CCl440Tetrahedral
PH331Trigonal pyramidal
H2S22Angular (bent)
NH331Trigonal pyramidal (bond angle 107 degree)
H2O22Bent (bond angle 104.5 degree)
CS220Linear (bond angle 180 degree, the maximum)
BF330Planar trigonal (bond angle 120 degree)

Hybridization

Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy to produce an equal number of new orbitals of the same energy, called hybrid orbitals.

  • sp3 hybridization in CH4: the 2s and three 2p orbitals of carbon mix to form four sp3 hybrid orbitals directed towards the corners of a tetrahedron; each overlaps with the 1s orbital of hydrogen, giving a tetrahedral molecule with 109.5 degree angles.
  • sp2 hybridization in C2H4: each carbon mixes its 2s and two 2p orbitals to form three sp2 hybrid orbitals in one plane at 120 degree, used for sigma bonds with two hydrogens and the other carbon. The unhybridized p orbital on each carbon overlaps sideways to form the pi bond of the C=C double bond.
  • Expected hybridization: BeCl2 — sp, linear; BF3 — sp2, planar trigonal; CH4 — sp3, tetrahedral; C2H2 — each carbon is sp, linear.

options: Lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair

lessons.title: Bond Characteristics
lessons.notes_html:
Bond energy, bond length and bond order describe the strength and size of a covalent bond, and together they decide many properties of the molecule.

Bond Energy

Bond energy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in a molecule; it is measured in KJ/mol and shows the strength of the bond. The H-F bond is very short and strongly polar due to the small size and high electronegativity of fluorine, so it has the highest bond energy among bonds like Cl-Cl, H-O and H-N. The bond energy of molecules possessing multiple bonds is high, because a multiple bond (double or triple) contains one sigma and one or two pi bonds, more energy is needed to break all of them together, and the atoms are also held closer.

Bond Length

Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms in a molecule, measured in Angstrom (A). It depends on the size of the atoms and the bond order: a higher bond order means a shorter bond length. For example, a C-C single bond is longer than a C=C double bond.

Bond Order

Bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons)/2. N2 has bond order 3 (triple bond) and O2 has bond order 2 (double bond).

Ionic Character

HF has greater ionic character than HCl because fluorine is much more electronegative than chlorine, so the electronegativity difference between H and F is larger than between H and Cl; hence the H-F bond is more polar.

Form one mole of a bond from atoms in solution

mcqs.why: Bond energy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in a molecule, and it shows bond strength.

Pi bonds alone are stronger than all sigma bonds
Multiple bonds contain no sigma bond
mcqs.why: A multiple bond contains one sigma and one or two pi bonds; more energy is needed to break all of them together and the atoms are held closer.

mcqs.why: Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms and is measured in Angstrom (A).

Lower bond order always gives a shorter bond

mcqs.why: N2 has bond order 3, a triple bond, while O2 has bond order 2, a double bond, as calculated from their MO electron counts.

Hydrogen is more electronegative than fluorine

mcqs.why: Fluorine is much more electronegative than chlorine, so the H-F electronegativity difference is larger and the H-F bond is more polar with greater ionic character.

lessons.title: Effect of Bonding on Physical and Chemical Properties
lessons.notes_html:
The type of bonding and the shape of a molecule decide its polarity, and polarity in turn decides properties such as solubility.

Dipole Moment and Geometry

The dipole moment of water is 1.85D but CO2 has zero dipole moment. Water has a bent shape, so the dipoles of the two O-H bonds do not cancel; they add up to give a resultant dipole moment of 1.85D, making water polar. Carbon dioxide is a linear molecule (O=C=O), in which the two equal C=O bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions, so they cancel each other completely and the net dipole moment of CO2 is zero. CCl4 also has zero dipole moment: it is a regular tetrahedron and the four equal C-Cl bond dipoles cancel each other. This shows that dipole moment depends not only on bond polarity but also on molecular geometry. The Debye is the practical unit of dipole moment: 1D = 3.33 x 10^-30 Cm.

Like Dissolves Like

Oil is insoluble in water but soluble in hexane. Oil is a non-polar covalent substance, while water is a polar solvent. According to the rule "like dissolves like", the polar water molecules attract each other strongly through hydrogen bonding and do not allow the non-polar oil molecules to mix, so oil forms a separate layer. Hexane is also non-polar, and the weak London forces between oil and hexane molecules are comparable with the forces within each liquid, so oil dissolves in hexane, just as non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.

mcqs.why: The lesson states that the dipole moment of water is 1.85D, because its bent shape prevents the O-H bond dipoles from cancelling.

mcqs.why: CO2 is linear (O=C=O), so the two equal C=O bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel each other completely.

mcqs.why: Like dissolves like means substances dissolve best in solvents of similar polarity, so non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.

mcqs.why: CO2 has a linear geometry, written O=C=O, which places the two bond dipoles in exactly opposite directions so they cancel.

mcqs.why: Water has a bent shape, so the dipoles of the two O-H bonds do not cancel; they add up to give a resultant dipole moment of 1.85D, making water polar.

lessons.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
The behaviour of gases is explained by the kinetic molecular theory, which pictures a gas as a large number of tiny particles in rapid motion.

Main Postulates of Kinetic Molecular Theory

  • A gas consists of a large number of tiny particles (molecules) which are far apart, so the actual volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
  • The molecules are in continuous rapid motion in all directions and collide with each other and with the walls of the container; these collisions are perfectly elastic.
  • There are no forces of attraction between the molecules.
  • The average kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
  • The pressure of the gas is produced by the collisions of molecules with the walls of the container.

Pressure and Its Units

Pressure is the force applied per unit area on the surface of an object; for a gas it results from collisions of molecules with the walls of the container. Its SI unit is the pascal (N/m2), and it is also measured in atmosphere, torr and mm of Hg, where 1 atm = 760 torr = 760 mmHg = 101325 pascal. Molar mass is a fixed property of a gas and does not depend on temperature.

options: Negligible compared with the volume of the gas
Equal to the volume of the gas
Greater than the volume of the container
mcqs.why: The molecules are far apart, so the actual volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.

options: Always accompanied by a chemical reaction
mcqs.why: The theory states that gas molecules collide with each other and with the walls of the container and these collisions are perfectly elastic.

options: There are strong forces of attraction between molecules
Molecules move only in one direction
Molecules are stationary at room temperature
There are no forces of attraction between the molecules
mcqs.why: One postulate is that there are no forces of attraction between the molecules of a gas.

mcqs.why: The average kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, according to the kinetic theory.

options: Collisions of molecules with the walls of the container
mcqs.why: Pressure of the gas is produced by the collisions of molecules with the walls of the container.

mcqs.why: Pressure is the force applied per unit area on the surface of an object; for a gas it results from molecular collisions with the walls.

mcqs.why: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (N/m2), though atmosphere, torr and mm of Hg are also used.

mcqs.why: The lesson gives 1 atm = 760 torr = 760 mmHg = 101325 pascal.

mcqs.why: Molar mass is a fixed property of a gas and does not depend on temperature, as stated at the end of the lesson.

lessons.title: Absolute Temperature and Charles's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Charles's law connects the volume of a gas with its temperature and leads to the idea of absolute zero.

Charles's Law

Charles's law states that the volume of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature when pressure is kept constant, V proportional to T. It is used to define absolute zero, the temperature at which the volume of a gas would become zero.

Absolute Zero

Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, 0 K or -273.15 degree C, at which the volume of an ideal gas would become zero. In practice all gases liquefy before reaching it, and at absolute zero the kinetic energy and motion of the particles are at their minimum. By Charles's law the volume of a gas becomes theoretically zero at 0 K, not at 0 degree C or 273 K.

Effect of Temperature and Pressure Together

From V proportional to T/P: if the Kelvin temperature of an ideal gas is doubled and the pressure is reduced to one half, doubling T doubles V and halving P doubles it again, so the volume becomes four times.

options: Directly proportional to its absolute temperature
Inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
mcqs.why: Charles's law states that the volume of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature when pressure is kept constant, V proportional to T.

mcqs.q: Charles's law is used to define:
mcqs.why: Charles's law is used to define absolute zero, the temperature at which the volume of a gas would become zero.

mcqs.why: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, 0 K or -273.15 degree C, at which the volume of an ideal gas would become zero.

mcqs.why: At absolute zero the kinetic energy and motion of the particles are at their minimum, and in practice all gases liquefy before reaching it.

mcqs.why: By Charles's law the volume of a gas becomes theoretically zero at 0 K, not at 0 degree C or 273 K.

mcqs.why: From V proportional to T/P: doubling T doubles V and halving P doubles it again, so working is 2 x 2 = 4, and the volume becomes four times.

mcqs.why: Charles's law applies when pressure is kept constant, while volume changes directly with absolute temperature.

mcqs.why: Since V is directly proportional to T at constant pressure, doubling T doubles V: V2/V1 = T2/T1 = 2/1 = 2.

mcqs.why: Working: V changes by factor (1/2 for halved T) divided by (2 for doubled P) = 1/4, so the volume becomes one quarter of the original.

options: Because all gases liquefy before reaching absolute zero
Because molecules gain volume at low temperature
Because Charles's law fails at all temperatures
mcqs.why: In practice all gases liquefy before reaching absolute zero, so the theoretical zero volume at 0 K is never actually attained by a real gas.

lessons.title: Avogadro's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Avogadro's law relates the volume of a gas to the number of its particles.

Statement of Avogadro's Law

Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases contain an equal number of moles (or molecules) at the same temperature and pressure; the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its number of moles when temperature and pressure are constant, V proportional to n.

Molar Volume

It follows that one mole of every ideal gas occupies the same volume at STP: the molar volume of oxygen gas is 22.4 dm3 at 0 degree C and 1 atm. Molar volume increases with temperature and decreases with pressure, so it is maximum at the highest temperature and lowest pressure, e.g. at 25 degree C and 1 atm rather than at 0 degree C and 2 atm.

options: Volumes proportional to their molar masses
mcqs.why: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases contain an equal number of moles (or molecules) at the same temperature and pressure.

mcqs.q: According to Avogadro's law, at constant temperature and pressure, volume is:
options: Inversely proportional to number of moles
Proportional to the square of the moles
Directly proportional to number of moles, V proportional to n
mcqs.why: Avogadro's law gives that the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its number of moles when temperature and pressure are constant, V proportional to n.

mcqs.why: One mole of every ideal gas occupies the same volume at STP, and the molar volume of oxygen gas is 22.4 dm3 at 0 degree C and 1 atm.

mcqs.why: The molar volume 22.4 dm3 is quoted at 0 degree C and 1 atm, which are the standard temperature and pressure conditions used in the lesson.

22.4 dm3, the same volume for every ideal gas
A volume equal to its molar mass in dm3
mcqs.why: It follows from Avogadro's law that one mole of every ideal gas occupies the same volume at STP, namely 22.4 dm3.

mcqs.why: Molar volume increases with temperature and decreases with pressure, so raising the temperature increases the molar volume.

mcqs.why: Molar volume decreases with pressure, so increasing the pressure decreases the molar volume of a gas.

options: 25 degree C and 1 atm rather than 0 degree C and 2 atm
mcqs.why: Molar volume is maximum at the highest temperature and lowest pressure, e.g. at 25 degree C and 1 atm rather than at 0 degree C and 2 atm.

mcqs.why: Since V is directly proportional to n, doubling n doubles V: V2/V1 = n2/n1 = 2/1 = 2, at constant temperature and pressure.

mcqs.q: Two equal volumes of O2 and CO2 at the same T and P contain:
options: More molecules of CO2 because it is heavier
More molecules of O2 because it is lighter
mcqs.why: By Avogadro's law, equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of moles or molecules, regardless of molar mass.

lessons.title: Ideal Gas Equation
lessons.notes_html:
Boyle's law, Charles's law and Avogadro's law combine into a single equation of state for an ideal gas.

Derivation of the General Gas Equation

Boyle's law gives V proportional to 1/P at constant T, and Charles's law gives V proportional to T at constant P. Combining them, V proportional to T/P, or PV proportional to T. For n moles this becomes:

PV = nRT

where R is the universal gas constant.

Value of R

At STP one mole occupies 22.4 dm3 at 1 atm and 273K, so R = PV/nT = (1 x 22.4)/(1 x 273) = 0.0821 atm dm3/mol.K. In SI units, R = (101325 Pa x 0.0224 m3)/(1 x 273) = 8.314 J/mol.K.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Gorakh hill station is the coldest area of Sindh province and has 83 KPa barometer pressure. What will be the pressure of this area in psi and atm units? Solution: 1 atm = 101.325 kPa, so P = 83/101.325 = 0.819 atm. In psi: 1 atm = 14.7 psi, so P = 0.819 x 14.7 = about 12.04 psi.

Numerical 2: Calculate the volume occupied by 8g of methane gas at 40 degree C and 842 torr pressure. Solution: Moles of CH4 = 8/16 = 0.5 mol. Pressure = 842/760 = 1.108 atm, and T = 40 + 273 = 313K. V = nRT/P = (0.5 x 0.0821 x 313)/1.108 = 11.58 dm3.

Numerical 3: At 35 degree C, oxygen gas in a cylinder has 456 cm3 volume and 0.85 atm pressure. Calculate the pressure when this oxygen gas is transferred to a 10 dm3 cylinder and cooled to 20 degree C. Solution: V1 = 0.456 dm3, T1 = 308K, T2 = 293K, V2 = 10 dm3. Using the combined gas law, P2 = P1V1T2/(V2T1) = (0.85 x 0.456 x 293)/(10 x 308) = 0.037 atm. The pressure falls greatly because the gas is expanded into a much larger volume.

Numerical 4: Four containers of equal volume are filled as follows: (i) 2.0g of H2 at 0 degree C (ii) 1.0g of H2 at 273 degree C (iii) 24g of O2 at 0 degree C (iv) 16g of CH4 at 273 degree C. Which container is at the greatest pressure and which at the lowest? Solution: For equal volumes, pressure is proportional to n x T. (i) n = 1 mol, T = 273K, nT = 273. (ii) n = 0.5 mol, T = 546K, nT = 273. (iii) n = 24/32 = 0.75 mol, T = 273K, nT = 204.75. (iv) n = 1 mol, T = 546K, nT = 546. Container (iv) has the greatest nT, so it is at the greatest pressure; container (iii) has the smallest nT, so it is at the lowest pressure.

lessons.title: Deviation from Ideal Gas Behaviour
lessons.notes_html:
No real gas obeys PV = nRT under all conditions. Real gases approach ideal behaviour only when their molecules are far apart and intermolecular forces are negligible.

Ideal Gas versus Real Gas

Ideal GasReal Gas
Obeys the gas laws and PV = nRT at all temperatures and pressuresObeys the van der Waals equation; shows ideal behaviour only at high temperature and low pressure
Molecules assumed to have no volumeMolecules occupy a finite volume
No intermolecular attractions assumedAttractive forces exist between molecules

Causes of Deviation

The causes of deviation are the two faulty assumptions of the kinetic theory: real gas molecules do occupy a finite volume, and attractive forces do exist between them.

  • At low temperature: the molecules move slowly, so attractions pull them together and the volume and pressure are less than expected.
  • At high pressure: the molecules are crowded close together, so their own volume cannot be neglected and the gas is less compressible than an ideal gas.
  • Ideal behaviour: a real gas reaches ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure. Among all real gases, helium acts most like an ideal gas at room temperature.

Real molecules occupy a finite volume and attractive forces exist between them

mcqs.why: Among all real gases, helium acts most like an ideal gas at room temperature, as stated in the lesson.

lessons.title: Van der Waals Equation
lessons.notes_html:
In order to modify the two conflicting postulates of the kinetic molecular theory regarding volumes of gas molecules and intermolecular attraction of gas molecules, the Dutch scientist J.D. van der Waal (1873) gave a mathematical solution by the correction in molecular volume and intermolecular forces. This is known as the van der Waal's equation.

Volume Correction

When pressure is applied to a gas, the molecules come closer to each other, and by continuous increase in pressure a point is reached when molecules cannot be compressed further, since repulsive forces are created. This indicates that gas molecules have a definite volume. Keeping in view the definite volume of gas molecules, van der Waal calculated the actual (free) volume of a gas as:

V = V(vessel) - nb

where V = free volume, V(vessel) = volume of the vessel in which gas molecules are present, n = number of moles, and b = excluded volume of gas molecules per mole. The value of b depends upon the size of gas molecules; b is not the actual volume of the gas but is assumed to be four times the actual volume of the molecules: b = 4V(molecule).

Pressure Correction

A molecule in the interior of the gas is completely surrounded and attracted by the other gas molecules, so the resultant attractive force on it is zero. However, as a molecule approaches to strike the wall of the vessel, it experiences a net inward pull due to the attractive forces of the molecules behind it, so the pressure produced on the wall is a little less than the pressure of an ideal gas molecule. The pressure drop PL is proportional to the number of particles per unit volume: PL = an^2/V^2, where a is a constant. Hence the ideal pressure is Pi = P + an^2/V^2.

The van der Waals Equation

Putting the corrected pressure and volume in the general gas equation:

(P + an^2/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT

If n = 1, the equation becomes (P + a/V^2)(V - b) = RT. Here a and b are van der Waal's constants. Since P = an^2/V^2 gives a = PV^2/n^2, the unit of a is atm dm6 mole-2; b represents the volume per mole of gas, so its unit is dm3/mol.

lessons.title: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressure
lessons.notes_html:
When two or more gases are mixed in one vessel, each gas contributes its own share to the total pressure.

Statement of Dalton's Law

Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a mixture of two or more non-reacting gases in a fixed volume enclosed container is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases:

P(total) = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...

The partial pressure of a gas is the pressure it would exert if it occupied the vessel alone, and it can be calculated from its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.

Practical Applications of Dalton's Law

  • Collecting a gas over water and correcting its pressure for water vapour: the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressure of the gas and the vapour pressure of water.
  • Calculating pressures in gas mixtures used in deep-sea diving.
  • Working out the composition of air and respiratory gases.
  • In industry, wherever gases are stored and mixed in cylinders.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: A 500 cm3 vessel contains H2 gas at 400 torr pressure and another 1 dm3 vessel contains O2 gas at 600 torr pressure. If under similar conditions of temperature these gases are transferred to a 2 dm3 empty vessel, calculate the pressure of the mixture. Solution: On transfer, each gas expands into 2 dm3, so find its partial pressure by Boyle's law. For H2: P = 400 x 0.5/2 = 100 torr. For O2: P = 600 x 1/2 = 300 torr. By Dalton's law, total pressure = 100 + 300 = 400 torr.

Numerical 2: 40 dm3 of hydrogen gas was collected over water at 831 torr pressure at 23 degree C. What would be the volume of dry hydrogen gas at standard conditions? The vapour pressure of water at 23 degree C is 21 torr. Solution: Pressure of dry H2 = 831 - 21 = 810 torr. T1 = 296K; at standard conditions P2 = 760 torr and T2 = 273K. V2 = P1V1T2/(T1P2) = (810 x 40 x 273)/(296 x 760) = about 39.3 dm3.

mcqs.why: Working: partial pressures are 100 torr for H2 and 300 torr for O2, so by Dalton's law total pressure = 100 + 300 = 400 torr.

lessons.title: Graham's Law of Diffusion and Effusion
lessons.notes_html:
Gases spread out and escape through small openings at rates that depend on their molar masses.

Diffusion and Effusion

  • Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of gases (or particles) due to their random molecular motion, so that they spread uniformly throughout the available space.
  • Effusion is the escape of a gas through a tiny hole or porous material into a region of lower pressure.

Graham's Law

Graham's law states that the rate of diffusion (or effusion) of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density or molar mass at constant temperature and pressure. Thus for two gases:

r1/r2 = sqrt(M2/M1)

Lighter gases like hydrogen diffuse much faster than heavier gases like oxygen: sqrt(32/2) = 4, so H2 diffuses 4 times faster than O2, a ratio of 4:1. C3H8 and CO2 diffuse at the same rate because both have molar mass 44 g/mol.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Compare the rates of diffusion of the following pairs of gases: (1) H2 and D2 (2) He and SO2 (3) SF6 and SO2. Solution: By Graham's law, rate ratio = sqrt(M of heavier gas / M of lighter gas). (1) H2 (M = 2) and D2 (M = 4): r(H2)/r(D2) = sqrt(4/2) = 1.41. (2) He (M = 4) and SO2 (M = 64): r(He)/r(SO2) = sqrt(64/4) = 4. (3) SF6 (M = 146) and SO2 (M = 64): r(SO2)/r(SF6) = sqrt(146/64) = 1.51, i.e. the lighter SO2 diffuses 1.51 times faster.

Numerical 2: If 16 cm3 of hydrogen effuses in 30 sec from a porous material, what volume of SO2 will effuse in the same time under similar conditions? Solution: Volume effused in the same time is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass. V(SO2) = V(H2) x sqrt(M of H2 / M of SO2) = 16 x sqrt(2/64) = 16/5.66 = 2.83 cm3. Only about 2.83 cm3 of SO2 effuses in 30 seconds because SO2 is much heavier than hydrogen.

mcqs.why: C3H8 and CO2 diffuse at the same rate because both have molar mass 44 g/mol, and Graham's law depends on molar mass.

mcqs.why: Working: V(SO2) = V(H2) x sqrt(M of H2 / M of SO2) = 16 x sqrt(2/64) = 16/5.66 = 2.83 cm3, because SO2 is much heavier than hydrogen.

lessons.title: Liquefaction of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Gases can be turned into liquids by compressing them and cooling them to very low temperatures; air itself can be liquefied in this way.

Liquid Air

Liquid air is ordinary air which, on compression and cooling to an extremely low temperature (about -190 degree C), becomes liquefied. It is a pale blue liquid mixture mainly of liquid nitrogen and liquid oxygen. Liquid air must be stored in special insulated vessels because it evaporates very quickly.

Uses of Liquid Air

  • It provides a very low temperature for scientific research and refrigeration.
  • Fractional distillation of liquid air gives nitrogen, oxygen and noble gases for industry and hospitals.
  • Liquid oxygen obtained from it is used in rockets, welding and medical treatment.

lessons.title: Fourth State of Matter: Plasma
lessons.notes_html:
Beyond solid, liquid and gas there is a fourth state of matter called plasma, found in the sun and in many modern devices.

What is Plasma?

Plasma is the fourth state of matter, consisting of a mixture of ions, electrons and un-ionized atoms and molecules. It is formed when a gas is heated to a very high temperature or subjected to a strong electric field, so that its atoms become ionized.

Significance of Plasma in Daily Life

  • Fluorescent tubes and neon sign lights work on plasma.
  • Plasma television screens use it to produce pictures.
  • Plasma torches are used for cutting metals.
  • The sun and other stars consist of plasma.
  • It is being studied for producing electricity by nuclear fusion.

lessons.title: Kinetic Molecular Interpretation of Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
In liquids the molecules are close together but not fixed; they are in constant motion and can slide over one another. This picture explains the familiar properties of liquids.

Kinetic Interpretation of Liquid Properties

  • Diffusion: liquid molecules are in constant motion and slowly intermingle with the molecules of another liquid, though diffusion is slower than in gases because the molecules are closer together.
  • Compression: liquid molecules are already closely packed with very little empty space, so liquids are almost incompressible.
  • Expansion: on heating, the kinetic energy of the molecules increases and they move slightly apart, so liquids expand much less than gases.
  • Molecular motion: liquid molecules do not have fixed positions; they slide over one another, which is why liquids can flow and take the shape of the container, while they possess a definite volume.

mcqs.q: Why is diffusion slower in liquids than in gases?
options: Liquid molecules are fixed in position
Liquid molecules have no kinetic energy
Liquid molecules are closer together, so they intermingle more slowly
Liquid molecules are heavier than all gas molecules
mcqs.why: Diffusion is slower in liquids because the molecules are closer together, even though they are in constant motion and slowly intermingle with another liquid.

options: Their molecules are already closely packed with very little empty space

mcqs.why: Liquids are almost incompressible because their molecules are already closely packed with very little empty space between them, so they cannot be pushed much closer.

options: Its molecules lose kinetic energy and contract greatly
Its molecules become fixed in position

Its molecules gain kinetic energy and move slightly apart, so it expands much less than a gas
mcqs.why: On heating, the kinetic energy of liquid molecules increases and they move slightly apart, so liquids expand, but much less than gases expand.

options: Their molecules are arranged in a rigid lattice

Close together but in constant motion
mcqs.why: In liquids the molecules are close together but not fixed; they are in constant motion and can slide over one another.

lessons.title: Inter-Molecular Forces in Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
The properties of a liquid are governed by the forces of attraction between its molecules. There are three major kinds of intermolecular forces in liquids.

Kinds of Intermolecular Forces

  • Dipole-dipole interactions: attractions between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another.
  • London dispersion forces: weak forces due to temporary dipoles, present in all molecules; the smallest molecule F2 has the weakest London forces, and a non-polar molecule experiences only London forces, which increase with molecular size.
  • Hydrogen bonding: the strongest of the three, found in molecules like H2O, NH3 and HF where hydrogen is bonded to F, O or N (it is absent in CH4, because carbon is not a highly electronegative atom).

Intermolecular Forces in HCl

HCl is a polar molecule with a permanent dipole, positive on hydrogen and negative on chlorine. In liquid HCl the positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of a neighbouring molecule, giving dipole-dipole interactions. In addition, weak London dispersion forces act between all the molecules due to temporary dipoles. Hydrogen bonding of the strong type (as in water) is absent in HCl because chlorine is large and less electronegative in effect.

Hydrogen Bond

A hydrogen bond is the force of attraction between a partially positively charged hydrogen atom in one molecule and a lone pair of a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) in another molecule. It is established when hydrogen is covalently bonded to such an electronegative atom, which pulls the shared electrons towards itself and leaves the hydrogen with a partial positive charge that attracts a neighbouring lone pair. In industry, hydrogen bonding explains the high solubility of substances like sugar and alcohol in water and is important in making adhesives, paints and fibres such as nylon. In biochemical processes it holds together the two strands of DNA, gives proteins their shapes, and is essential in enzyme action and the working of medicines.

Hydrogen Bonding in Water and the Anomalous Behaviour of Water

In water, the hydrogen atom of one molecule, being partially positive, is attracted to a lone pair of the oxygen atom of another molecule, forming a hydrogen bond. Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, building an open, cage-like structure in ice. Because of this open structure, ice is less dense than liquid water and floats on it. Water also expands below 4 degree C, so its density is maximum at 4 degree C; this anomalous behaviour protects aquatic life, as ice forms only at the surface of ponds in winter. Hydrogen bonding is also why the boiling point of water (100 degree C) is much higher than that of H2S, which has no hydrogen bonding: the strong hydrogen bonds need extra heat to break.

Volatility and Intermolecular Forces

Volatility increases as intermolecular forces become weaker, because molecules escape more easily from the surface. Glycerin has three -OH groups per molecule and very extensive hydrogen bonding, so it is much less volatile than water. Petrol consists of non-polar hydrocarbon molecules held only by weak London forces, so its molecules escape even more easily than water molecules. Hence the order of volatility is petrol > water > glycerin, exactly following the decreasing strength of intermolecular forces.
