options: Up to four; an open, cage-like structure in ice
mcqs.why: Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, building an open, cage-like structure in ice, which is why ice is less dense than liquid water.

mcqs.q: The anomalous behaviour of water described in the lesson is that:
options: Water is densest at 0 degree C
Water expands below 4 degree C, so its density is maximum at 4 degree C
Ice is denser than liquid water and sinks
Water boils below 100 degree C at normal pressure
mcqs.why: Water expands below 4 degree C, so its density is maximum at 4 degree C; this anomalous behaviour protects aquatic life because ice forms only at the surface of ponds in winter.

mcqs.q: Why is the boiling point of water (100 degree C) much higher than that of H2S?
options: H2S has stronger hydrogen bonds than water
Water molecules are smaller than H2S molecules
H2S is non-polar and water is ionic
Water has strong hydrogen bonds that need extra heat to break, while H2S has no hydrogen bonding
mcqs.why: The boiling point of water is much higher than that of H2S because water has strong hydrogen bonds needing extra heat to break, while H2S has no hydrogen bonding.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of volatility, and why?
options: Glycerin is most volatile, then water, then petrol, because glycerin has most -OH groups
Water is most volatile because it hydrogen bonds most strongly
Petrol is most volatile, then water, then glycerin, because intermolecular forces decrease in that order
mcqs.why: The order of volatility is petrol, then water, then glycerin: petrol has only weak London forces, water hydrogen bonds, and glycerin has three -OH groups with very extensive hydrogen bonding, so volatility increases as intermolecular forces weaken.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
Surface tension, viscosity, evaporation and boiling are the observable physical properties of liquids, and all of them arise from intermolecular forces.

Surface Tension

Surface tension is the force responsible for the tension at the surface of a liquid; it is the energy required to stretch (increase) the surface by unit area. The surface molecules are pulled inwards by the molecules below them, so the surface behaves like a stretched elastic membrane; for example, a needle can float on water and insects can walk on it. Its unit is N/m (or J/m2). Surface tension decreases with rise in temperature and decreases when detergents or impurities are added, while strong intermolecular forces, such as hydrogen bonding and metallic bonding, give high surface tension as in water and mercury. Mercury shows the maximum surface tension because of its very strong cohesive (metallic) forces. A falling drop of a liquid is spherical because surface tension pulls the surface into the smallest possible area.

Meniscus

When cohesive forces within a liquid are stronger than adhesive forces between the liquid and glass, the liquid forms a convex (upward) meniscus, as mercury does. In mercury cohesive forces are stronger than adhesive forces with glass, so the surface curves upward. When adhesive forces are stronger, the meniscus is concave, as with water.

Viscosity: Why Honey is More Viscous than Water

Viscosity is the internal resistance to the flow of a liquid, caused by friction between its layers. Honey is more viscous than water because its molecules (large sugar molecules such as glucose and fructose) are big, irregular and strongly attracted to each other by extensive hydrogen bonding. These large molecules entangle and cannot slide past one another easily, so honey flows very slowly. Water molecules are small, and although they also hydrogen bond, the layers slip over each other with much less resistance. Viscosity also decreases on heating, which is why warm honey flows faster than cold honey.

Evaporation and Boiling Point

  • Water spilled on the floor evaporates faster than the same amount of water in a container because spilled water has a much larger surface area, and evaporation takes place from the surface.
  • Evaporation is a cooling process: the molecules with the highest kinetic energy escape, lowering the average energy and temperature of the remaining liquid. The cooling felt after a bath is due to evaporation of water from the skin.
  • The boiling point of a liquid remains constant although heat is continuously supplied, because at the boiling point the supplied heat is used to overcome intermolecular forces (latent heat) instead of raising the temperature.
  • Boiling points of different liquids may be different at the same external pressure due to intermolecular forces; stronger forces give a higher boiling point.
  • In a pressure cooker the increased pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100 degree C, so cooking time is reduced.

mcqs.q: Surface tension is best defined as:
options: The internal resistance to flow of a liquid
The rate at which a liquid evaporates
The pressure at which a liquid boils
The energy required to stretch (increase) the surface of a liquid by unit area
mcqs.why: Surface tension is the force responsible for the tension at the surface of a liquid; it is the energy required to stretch the surface by unit area.

mcqs.q: The unit of surface tension is:
mcqs.why: Surface tension is measured in N/m, which is equivalent to J/m2, because it is energy required per unit increase in surface area.

mcqs.q: Why can a needle float on water and insects walk on it?
options: Surface molecules are pulled inwards, so the surface behaves like a stretched elastic membrane
Water molecules at the surface have no attractions
mcqs.why: The surface molecules are pulled inwards by the molecules below them, so the surface behaves like a stretched elastic membrane that can support a needle or an insect.

mcqs.q: How does surface tension change with rise in temperature and with detergents?
options: It decreases with temperature but increases with detergents
It decreases with rise in temperature and decreases when detergents or impurities are added
mcqs.why: Surface tension decreases with rise in temperature and also decreases when detergents or impurities are added to the liquid.

mcqs.q: Which liquid shows the maximum surface tension, and why?
options: Mercury, because of its very strong cohesive (metallic) forces
Water, because of hydrogen bonding alone
Glycerin, because it is most viscous
Petrol, because of weak London forces
mcqs.why: Mercury shows the maximum surface tension because of its very strong cohesive forces, the metallic forces between its atoms.

mcqs.q: Why is a falling drop of a liquid spherical?
options: Gravity pulls it into a sphere
Surface tension pulls the surface into the smallest possible area
mcqs.why: A falling drop is spherical because surface tension pulls the surface into the smallest possible area, and a sphere has the smallest surface area for its volume.

mcqs.q: Mercury forms a convex (upward) meniscus in glass because:
options: Adhesive forces with glass are stronger than cohesive forces
Mercury does not wet any surface for temperature reasons
Its surface tension falls to zero in glass
Cohesive forces within mercury are stronger than adhesive forces between mercury and glass
mcqs.why: When cohesive forces within a liquid are stronger than adhesive forces between the liquid and glass, the liquid forms a convex meniscus, as mercury does.

mcqs.q: Water forms a concave meniscus in glass because:
options: Its cohesive forces are stronger than its adhesive forces
Its adhesive forces with glass are stronger than its cohesive forces
It evaporates from the edges first
mcqs.why: When adhesive forces are stronger than cohesive forces, the meniscus is concave, as with water in glass, where water is attracted to the glass more strongly.

mcqs.q: Viscosity is defined as:
options: The energy needed to increase surface area
The internal resistance to the flow of a liquid, caused by friction between its layers
The temperature at which vapour pressure equals air pressure
The loss of molecules from the surface
mcqs.why: Viscosity is the internal resistance to the flow of a liquid, caused by friction between its layers as they slide past one another.

mcqs.q: Why is honey more viscous than water?
options: Honey contains large sugar molecules that entangle and are strongly attracted by extensive hydrogen bonding
Honey molecules are small and move freely
Water has stronger hydrogen bonding than honey
Honey has a higher surface tension than mercury
mcqs.why: Honey is more viscous than water because its large sugar molecules, such as glucose and fructose, are irregular, entangle, and are strongly attracted to each other by extensive hydrogen bonding, so they cannot slide past easily.

mcqs.q: Why does warm honey flow faster than cold honey?
mcqs.why: Viscosity decreases on heating, which is why warm honey flows faster than cold honey; the layers slip over each other with less resistance when warm.

mcqs.q: Water spilled on the floor evaporates faster than the same amount in a container because:
options: Spilled water has a much larger surface area and evaporation takes place from the surface
The container raises the boiling point
Spilled water has stronger intermolecular forces
mcqs.why: Spilled water evaporates faster because it has a much larger surface area, and evaporation takes place from the surface of the liquid.

mcqs.q: Why is evaporation a cooling process?
options: All molecules escape at the same rate
Evaporation adds energy to the liquid
Condensation occurs at the same time in equal amount
The molecules with the highest kinetic energy escape, lowering the average energy and temperature of the remaining liquid
mcqs.why: Evaporation cools because the molecules with the highest kinetic energy escape, lowering the average energy and temperature of the remaining liquid, as in the cooling felt after a bath.

mcqs.q: Why does the boiling point remain constant although heat is continuously supplied?
options: No heat is absorbed at the boiling point
The supplied heat is used to raise the temperature faster
The supplied heat is used to overcome intermolecular forces (latent heat) instead of raising the temperature
The liquid stops evaporating at its boiling point
mcqs.why: At the boiling point the supplied heat is used to overcome intermolecular forces as latent heat instead of raising the temperature, so the boiling point remains constant.

mcqs.q: In a pressure cooker, food cooks faster because:
options: Increased pressure lowers the boiling point of water
Increased pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100 degree C, reducing cooking time
Steam cannot escape, so evaporation stops
mcqs.why: In a pressure cooker the increased pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100 degree C, so the food is cooked at a higher temperature and cooking time is reduced.

lessons.title: Energetics of Phase Change
lessons.notes_html:
Every change of state involves a definite amount of heat per mole of the substance.

Molar Heats of Phase Change

  • Molar heat of fusion is the amount of heat required to convert one mole of a solid completely into liquid at its melting point; for water it is +6.02 KJ/mol.
  • Molar heat of vapourization is the heat required to convert one mole of a liquid into its vapours at its boiling point; for water it is 40.7 KJ/mol.
  • Molar heat of sublimation is the heat absorbed when one mole of a solid changes directly into vapours without passing through the liquid state. It is equal to the sum of the molar heat of fusion and the molar heat of vapourization.

Sublimation is an endothermic process, and evaporation also absorbs heat from the surroundings, so it is endothermic too (not exothermic); evaporation is the reverse process of condensation, occurs at all temperatures, and causes a cooling effect.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of fusion is the heat required to:
options: Convert one mole of liquid into vapour at its boiling point
Convert one mole of solid completely into liquid at its melting point
Convert one mole of solid directly into vapour
Raise one mole of liquid by 1 degree C
mcqs.why: Molar heat of fusion is the amount of heat required to convert one mole of a solid completely into liquid at its melting point.

mcqs.q: The molar heat of fusion of water is:
mcqs.why: For water the molar heat of fusion is +6.02 KJ/mol, the heat absorbed to convert one mole of ice completely into liquid water at its melting point.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of vapourization is the heat required to:
options: Convert one mole of solid into liquid at its melting point
Convert one mole of liquid into its vapours at its boiling point
mcqs.why: Molar heat of vapourization is the heat required to convert one mole of a liquid into its vapours at its boiling point.

mcqs.q: The molar heat of vapourization of water is:
mcqs.why: For water the molar heat of vapourization is 40.7 KJ/mol, much larger than its molar heat of fusion of 6.02 KJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of sublimation is the heat absorbed when:
options: One mole of liquid evaporates at room temperature
One mole of vapour condenses to liquid
One mole of solid changes directly into vapours without passing through the liquid state
One mole of solid melts at its melting point
mcqs.why: Molar heat of sublimation is the heat absorbed when one mole of a solid changes directly into vapours without passing through the liquid state.

mcqs.q: Molar heat of sublimation is equal to:
options: Molar heat of vapourization minus molar heat of fusion
Molar heat of fusion divided by molar heat of vapourization
The sum of the molar heat of fusion and the molar heat of vapourization
mcqs.why: Molar heat of sublimation equals the sum of the molar heat of fusion and the molar heat of vapourization, because the solid must effectively melt and then vapourize.

mcqs.q: Sublimation and evaporation are both:
options: Processes that occur only at the boiling point
Endothermic processes that absorb heat from the surroundings
mcqs.why: Sublimation is an endothermic process, and evaporation also absorbs heat from the surroundings, so evaporation is endothermic too, not exothermic.

mcqs.q: Evaporation is the reverse process of:
mcqs.why: Evaporation is the reverse process of condensation; it occurs at all temperatures and causes a cooling effect as the most energetic molecules escape.

mcqs.q: Using the values for water (fusion +6.02 KJ/mol, vapourization 40.7 KJ/mol), the molar heat of sublimation of ice is:
mcqs.why: Molar heat of sublimation = molar heat of fusion + molar heat of vapourization = 6.02 + 40.7 = 46.72 KJ/mol for water, as shown by adding the two given values.

mcqs.q: Which statement about evaporation is correct?
options: It absorbs heat, occurs at all temperatures and causes cooling
It is exothermic and warms the surroundings
It occurs only at the boiling point
It is the same process as sublimation
mcqs.why: Evaporation absorbs heat from the surroundings so it is endothermic, it occurs at all temperatures, and it causes a cooling effect on the remaining liquid.

lessons.title: Liquid Crystals
lessons.notes_html:
Liquid crystals are a state of matter between liquids and crystalline solids, widely used in display devices.

What are Liquid Crystals?

In liquid crystals the molecules keep an ordered arrangement like a crystal but can still flow like a liquid.

Compared with LiquidsCompared with Crystalline Solids
Their molecules are arranged in a regular direction, which makes them show optical properties such as double refractionThey have no rigid three-dimensional lattice
They flow and change shape like liquidsThey melt over a range instead of a sharp melting point, and can flow and change shape

Liquid crystals are widely used in LCD displays of watches, calculators, ATM machines and computer screens.

mcqs.q: Liquid crystals are a state of matter:
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are a state of matter between liquids and crystalline solids, widely used in display devices.

mcqs.q: In liquid crystals, the molecules:
options: Keep an ordered arrangement like a crystal but can still flow like a liquid
Are completely random like a gas
mcqs.why: In liquid crystals the molecules keep an ordered arrangement like a crystal but can still flow like a liquid, combining properties of both states.

mcqs.q: Compared with ordinary liquids, liquid crystals show optical properties such as double refraction because:
options: They melt at a sharp point
Their molecules are arranged in a regular direction
mcqs.why: Their molecules are arranged in a regular direction, which makes liquid crystals show optical properties such as double refraction, unlike ordinary liquids.

mcqs.q: Compared with crystalline solids, liquid crystals:
mcqs.why: Compared with crystalline solids, liquid crystals have no rigid three-dimensional lattice, so they are not rigid solids even though their molecules are ordered.

mcqs.q: Liquid crystals behave like liquids in that they:
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals flow and change shape like liquids, even though their molecules keep an ordered arrangement like those of a crystal.

mcqs.q: On heating, liquid crystals melt:
options: At one sharp melting point like a pure crystal
Over a range instead of a sharp melting point
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals melt over a range instead of a sharp melting point, and they can flow and change shape during that range.

mcqs.q: Liquid crystals are widely used in:
options: LCD displays of watches, calculators, ATM machines and computer screens
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are widely used in LCD displays of watches, calculators, ATM machines and computer screens, because their ordered molecules respond in displays.

mcqs.q: Which property belongs to liquid crystals rather than to crystalline solids?
options: A single sharp melting point in every case
Ability to flow and change shape while keeping molecular order
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals can flow and change shape while keeping an ordered molecular arrangement, whereas crystalline solids have a rigid lattice and fixed particles.

mcqs.q: Which property belongs to liquid crystals rather than to ordinary liquids?
options: No order of any kind among molecules
Flow in all directions with random molecules
Molecules arranged in a regular direction, giving double refraction
mcqs.why: Unlike ordinary liquids, liquid crystals have molecules arranged in a regular direction, which gives optical properties such as double refraction.

mcqs.q: A display device that uses liquid crystals is:
mcqs.why: LCD displays of computer screens, watches, calculators and ATM machines use liquid crystals, whose ordered but flowing molecules make the display work.

lessons.title: Kinetic Molecular Interpretation of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
In solids the particles are tightly packed in fixed positions with very strong attractive forces between them, which explains their rigidity and definite shape.

Why the Compressibility of Solids is Nearly Zero

In solids the particles are already tightly packed together with very small empty spaces and strong attractive forces between them. There is almost no room for the particles to be pushed closer, so the compressibility of solids is nearly zero.

Why Some Solids are Sublime in Nature

Some solids, like iodine, naphthalene and camphor, have very weak intermolecular forces between their particles. On heating, their surface particles gain enough energy to escape directly into the vapour state without melting first. Such solids are said to be sublime in nature. Sublimation is the direct conversion of a solid into gas (vapours) on heating, without passing through the liquid state.

Melting Point

Melting point is the fixed temperature at which a solid changes into liquid at atmospheric pressure. Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point, while amorphous solids melt over a range of temperature.

mcqs.q: Why are solids rigid with a definite shape?
options: Their particles are tightly packed in fixed positions with very strong attractive forces
Their particles are far apart and move freely
Their particles have no attractive forces
Their particles slide over one another
mcqs.why: In solids the particles are tightly packed in fixed positions with very strong attractive forces between them, which explains their rigidity and definite shape.

mcqs.q: The compressibility of solids is nearly zero because:
options: Their particles are in constant rapid motion
They melt over a range of temperature
Their particles are already tightly packed with very small empty spaces and strong attractive forces
mcqs.why: There is almost no room for the tightly packed particles of a solid to be pushed closer, so the compressibility of solids is nearly zero.

mcqs.q: Solids such as iodine, naphthalene and camphor are sublime in nature because:
options: They have very strong intermolecular forces
They have very weak intermolecular forces, so surface particles escape directly into vapour on heating
mcqs.why: Some solids are sublime because they have very weak intermolecular forces; on heating, their surface particles gain enough energy to escape directly into the vapour state without melting first.

mcqs.q: Sublimation is defined as:
options: Melting of a solid at a fixed temperature
Direct conversion of a solid into gas (vapours) on heating, without passing through the liquid state
Conversion of a gas directly into a liquid
Freezing of a liquid into a solid
mcqs.why: Sublimation is the direct conversion of a solid into gas (vapours) on heating, without passing through the liquid state, as shown by iodine, naphthalene and camphor.

mcqs.q: Melting point is:
options: The temperature at which a liquid boils
The temperature at which a solid sublimes
The fixed temperature at which a solid changes into liquid at atmospheric pressure
mcqs.why: Melting point is the fixed temperature at which a solid changes into liquid at atmospheric pressure; crystalline solids show this as a sharp value.

mcqs.q: Crystalline solids differ from amorphous solids in melting behaviour because crystalline solids:
options: Melt over a range of temperature
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point, while amorphous solids melt over a range of temperature, reflecting their ordered particle arrangement.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only sublime solids named in the lesson?
mcqs.why: Iodine, naphthalene and camphor are the sublime solids named in the lesson; their weak intermolecular forces let them pass directly into vapour on heating.

mcqs.q: On heating a sublime solid, its surface particles:
options: First melt into a liquid and then boil
Gain enough energy to escape directly into the vapour state without melting first
mcqs.why: On heating, the surface particles of a sublime solid gain enough energy to escape directly into the vapour state without melting first.

mcqs.q: The strong attractive forces and fixed positions in solids explain:
options: Their ability to flow like liquids
Their lack of a melting point
mcqs.why: Very strong attractive forces between tightly packed particles in fixed positions explain why solids are rigid and keep a definite shape.

mcqs.q: Amorphous solids, in contrast to crystalline solids, melt:
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids melt over a range of temperature, while crystalline solids have a sharp melting point at atmospheric pressure.

lessons.title: Types of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Solids are of two main types, crystalline and amorphous, according to the arrangement of their particles.

Crystalline and Amorphous Solids

Crystalline SolidsAmorphous Solids
Particles arranged in a definite, regular latticeParticles randomly arranged
Sharp melting pointMelt over a range of temperature
Definite geometrical shapes, e.g. NaCl and alumNo definite shape, e.g. glass and rubber
Anisotropic behaviourIsotropic behaviour

Alum is a crystalline solid because it has a definite geometrical shape, sharp melting point and an ordered lattice; glass, plastic and rubber are amorphous.

mcqs.q: In crystalline solids, the particles are arranged:
options: As free molecules in a liquid
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a definite, regular lattice, giving them sharp melting points and definite geometrical shapes.

mcqs.q: In amorphous solids, the particles are:
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids have particles randomly arranged, so they have no definite shape and melt over a range of temperature, like glass and rubber.

mcqs.q: Which pair of melting behaviours is correct?
options: Crystalline: melts over a range; amorphous: sharp melting point
Crystalline: sharp melting point; amorphous: melts over a range of temperature
Both melt over the same range
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point, whereas amorphous solids melt over a range of temperature because their particles are randomly arranged.

mcqs.q: Examples of crystalline solids with definite geometrical shapes are:
mcqs.why: NaCl and alum are crystalline solids with definite geometrical shapes, an ordered lattice and a sharp melting point.

mcqs.q: Examples of amorphous solids are:
mcqs.why: Glass and rubber are amorphous solids: their particles are randomly arranged, they have no definite shape and they melt over a range.

mcqs.q: Crystalline solids show which type of behaviour?
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids show anisotropic behaviour because of their regular particle arrangement, while amorphous solids are isotropic.

mcqs.q: Amorphous solids are isotropic because:
options: Their regular lattice is the same in all directions
They have a sharp melting point
Their random arrangement is the same in all directions
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids are isotropic because their random arrangement is the same in all directions, unlike the ordered arrangement in crystalline solids.

mcqs.q: Why is alum classified as a crystalline solid?
options: It melts over a range and has no shape
It has a definite geometrical shape, sharp melting point and an ordered lattice
mcqs.why: Alum is a crystalline solid because it has a definite geometrical shape, a sharp melting point and an ordered lattice of particles.

mcqs.q: Glass, plastic and rubber are classified as:
mcqs.why: Glass, plastic and rubber are amorphous solids, with randomly arranged particles, no definite shape and melting over a range of temperature.

mcqs.q: Solids are classified into crystalline and amorphous types according to:
mcqs.why: Solids are of two main types, crystalline and amorphous, according to the arrangement of their particles: regular lattice in crystalline and random in amorphous solids.

lessons.title: Properties of Crystalline Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Because their particles are arranged in a regular order, crystalline solids show special properties such as anisotropy, and many elements show allotropy and polymorphism.

Anisotropy

Anisotropy is the property of a substance of showing different values of certain physical properties, such as electrical conduction, thermal expansion and refractive index, when measured in different directions. Crystalline solids show anisotropy because their particles are arranged in a regular order, and the arrangement is different along different directions. For example, graphite conducts electricity parallel to its layers but not perpendicular to them, so graphite is anisotropic. Amorphous solids are isotropic because their random arrangement is the same in all directions.

Allotropy

Allotropy is the phenomenon in which the same element exists in two or more different crystal structures (forms) in the same physical state, e.g. diamond and graphite.

Transition Temperature

The transition temperature is the temperature at which two allotropic forms of the same element co-exist in equilibrium; below and above it, one or the other form is more stable. For example, rhombic sulphur is stable below 96 degree C and monoclinic sulphur above it, so 96 degree C (369K) is the transition temperature of sulphur, and both forms co-exist there. Another example is tin: white (metallic) tin changes into grey (powdery) tin below 13.2 degree C, which is its transition temperature. At the transition temperature the two forms have equal stability.

Polymorphism and Its Relation to Allotropy

Polymorphism is the phenomenon in which a solid substance exists in more than one crystalline shape (form) under different conditions of temperature and pressure. Allotropy is the same phenomenon applied to an element: when an element exists in two or more crystalline forms, the forms are called allotropes. Thus allotropy is a special case of polymorphism for elements. For example, carbon shows allotropy as diamond and graphite; sulphur is polymorphic (allotropic) as rhombic and monoclinic sulphur. Compounds can also be polymorphic, e.g. calcium carbonate as calcite and aragonite. Isomorphism is different: it is the phenomenon in which different solid substances exist in the same crystalline structure, e.g. NaCl and MgO, which both crystallize in the same cubic (rock-salt) structure and so have the same geometrical shapes.

mcqs.q: Anisotropy is the property of showing:
options: The same value of a property in all directions
Different values of certain physical properties, such as electrical conduction, thermal expansion and refractive index, in different directions
Two crystal forms of the same element
mcqs.why: Anisotropy is showing different values of certain physical properties, such as electrical conduction, thermal expansion and refractive index, when measured in different directions, due to the regular order in crystalline solids.

mcqs.q: Graphite is anisotropic because it:
options: Conducts electricity equally in all directions
Conducts electricity parallel to its layers but not perpendicular to them
mcqs.why: Graphite conducts electricity parallel to its layers but not perpendicular to them, so graphite is anisotropic, a property of crystalline solids with regular arrangement.

mcqs.q: Amorphous solids are isotropic because:
options: Their particles form a regular lattice
Their random arrangement is the same in all directions
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids are isotropic because their random arrangement is the same in all directions, so a property has the same value in every direction.

mcqs.q: Allotropy is the phenomenon in which:
options: The same element exists in two or more different crystal structures in the same physical state, e.g. diamond and graphite
Different substances share the same crystal structure
A compound exists in two liquid forms
An element changes its atomic number
mcqs.why: Allotropy is the phenomenon in which the same element exists in two or more different crystal structures (forms) in the same physical state, for example diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.

mcqs.q: Transition temperature is the temperature at which:
options: A solid melts into a liquid
Two allotropic forms of the same element co-exist in equilibrium and have equal stability
mcqs.why: The transition temperature is the temperature at which two allotropic forms of the same element co-exist in equilibrium; below and above it, one or the other form is more stable, and at it both have equal stability.

mcqs.q: For sulphur, the transition temperature is 96 degree C (369K) because:
options: Rhombic sulphur melts at 96 degree C
Monoclinic sulphur is stable at all temperatures
Rhombic sulphur is stable below 96 degree C and monoclinic sulphur above it, and both co-exist there
mcqs.why: Rhombic sulphur is stable below 96 degree C and monoclinic sulphur above it, so 96 degree C (369K) is the transition temperature of sulphur and both forms co-exist there.

mcqs.q: The transition temperature of tin relates to the change:
options: Grey tin changes into diamond above 13.2 degree C
White tin melts at 13.2 degree C
White (metallic) tin changes into grey (powdery) tin below 13.2 degree C
mcqs.why: White (metallic) tin changes into grey (powdery) tin below 13.2 degree C, which is the transition temperature of tin, where the two forms co-exist in equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Polymorphism is the phenomenon in which:
options: A solid substance exists in more than one crystalline shape under different conditions of temperature and pressure
An element has only one crystal form
A liquid forms crystals on cooling
mcqs.why: Polymorphism is the phenomenon in which a solid substance exists in more than one crystalline shape (form) under different conditions of temperature and pressure.

mcqs.q: How is allotropy related to polymorphism?
options: Allotropy is a special case of polymorphism applied to an element; compounds can also be polymorphic, e.g. calcium carbonate as calcite and aragonite
Polymorphism is a special case of allotropy for compounds only
mcqs.why: Allotropy is a special case of polymorphism for elements: when an element exists in two or more crystalline forms they are allotropes, and compounds can also be polymorphic, for example calcium carbonate as calcite and aragonite.

mcqs.q: Isomorphism is different from polymorphism because isomorphism is:
options: Different solid substances existing in the same crystalline structure, e.g. NaCl and MgO in the cubic rock-salt structure
One substance existing in many crystal forms
An element existing in two forms
A solid melting over a range
mcqs.why: Isomorphism is the phenomenon in which different solid substances exist in the same crystalline structure, for example NaCl and MgO both crystallize in the same cubic (rock-salt) structure.

lessons.title: Types of Crystalline Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Crystalline solids are classified into ionic, covalent, metallic and molecular types according to the particles that build the lattice and the forces between them.

Ionic Solids

  • They are hard and brittle because of strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
  • They have high melting and boiling points.
  • They do not conduct electricity in the solid state but conduct when molten or in aqueous solution, because the ions become free to move.
  • They are soluble in polar solvents like water but insoluble in non-polar solvents.

In NaCl, each Na+ ion is surrounded octahedrally by six Cl- ions, and each Cl- ion by six Na+ ions (6:6 coordination).

Covalent Solids: Diamond and Graphite

Diamond is a covalent (network) solid: every carbon atom is joined to four others by covalent bonds in a giant network. Diamond is a non-conductor of electricity because each carbon atom uses all four of its valence electrons in covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons to carry current. In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to only three others in flat layers, and the fourth electron of each atom is spare (delocalized) over the layer. These free electrons can move along the layers when a voltage is applied, so graphite conducts electricity, but only parallel to its layers, making it anisotropic.

Metallic Solids

Metallic solids consist of positive metal ions (kernels) arranged in a regular lattice, surrounded by a sea of free, delocalized valence electrons; the attraction between the kernels and this electron sea is the metallic bond. They are generally hard, lustrous, malleable and ductile, and have high melting points and densities. They conduct electricity because the free electrons can move through the lattice and carry charge when a voltage is applied. They conduct heat because these mobile electrons quickly transfer kinetic energy from the hot part to the cold part of the metal. Examples are iron, copper, aluminium and sodium.

Molecular Solids

Molecular solids consist of individual molecules held together only by weak intermolecular forces such as London forces, dipole-dipole attractions or hydrogen bonds, while the covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong. Very little energy is needed to overcome these weak forces, so molecular solids are soft and possess low melting points: ice (whose molecules are held by hydrogen bonds), solid CO2 (dry ice) and naphthalene are all soft solids with low melting or sublimation points, unlike ionic or covalent network solids.

mcqs.q: Ionic solids are hard and brittle because of:
options: Free electrons moving through the lattice
Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
mcqs.why: Ionic solids are hard and brittle because of strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions, which also give them high melting and boiling points.

mcqs.q: Ionic solids conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution, but not as solids, because:
options: When molten or dissolved, the ions become free to move; in the solid they are fixed
In the solid the ions are free to move
Electrons are delocalized in ionic solids
Water creates new ions in every ionic solid
mcqs.why: Ionic solids do not conduct in the solid state but conduct when molten or in aqueous solution, because the ions then become free to move and carry charge.

mcqs.q: Ionic solids are generally:
options: Soluble in non-polar solvents and insoluble in water
Soluble in polar solvents like water but insoluble in non-polar solvents
mcqs.why: Ionic solids are soluble in polar solvents like water but insoluble in non-polar solvents, a consequence of the strong electrostatic forces between their ions.

mcqs.q: In NaCl, the coordination is 6:6 because:
options: Each Na+ is surrounded by four Cl- ions
Each Na+ ion is surrounded octahedrally by six Cl- ions, and each Cl- ion by six Na+ ions
Each ion is surrounded by eight ions of the same charge
Na+ and Cl- share six covalent bonds
mcqs.why: In NaCl, each Na+ ion is surrounded octahedrally by six Cl- ions, and each Cl- ion by six Na+ ions, giving 6:6 coordination in the ionic lattice.

mcqs.q: Diamond is a non-conductor of electricity because:
options: It has delocalized electrons over layers
Each carbon atom uses all four valence electrons in covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons
It contains ions that cannot move
It is a molecular solid with weak forces
mcqs.why: Diamond is a covalent network solid in which every carbon atom is joined to four others and uses all four valence electrons in covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons to carry current.

mcqs.q: Graphite conducts electricity, but only parallel to its layers, because:
options: Each carbon is bonded to four others with no spare electrons
Each carbon is bonded to only three others, and the fourth electron is delocalized over the layer and can move along it
mcqs.why: In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to only three others in flat layers, and the fourth electron of each atom is delocalized over the layer, so current flows parallel to the layers, making graphite anisotropic.

mcqs.q: A metallic solid consists of:
options: Positive metal ions (kernels) in a regular lattice surrounded by a sea of free, delocalized valence electrons
Individual molecules held by weak forces
Carbon atoms in a giant network only
mcqs.why: Metallic solids consist of positive metal ions (kernels) arranged in a regular lattice, surrounded by a sea of free, delocalized valence electrons; the attraction between kernels and this electron sea is the metallic bond.

mcqs.q: Metals conduct heat and electricity because:
options: Their ions move freely through the solid
Their molecules are held only by London forces
Their free electrons move through the lattice, carrying charge and quickly transferring kinetic energy from hot to cold parts
mcqs.why: Metallic solids conduct electricity because free electrons move through the lattice and carry charge, and they conduct heat because these mobile electrons quickly transfer kinetic energy from the hot part to the cold part.

mcqs.q: In molecular solids, the particles are held together by:
options: Strong covalent bonds between all molecules
Only weak intermolecular forces such as London forces, dipole-dipole attractions or hydrogen bonds, while covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong
mcqs.why: Molecular solids consist of individual molecules held together only by weak intermolecular forces such as London forces, dipole-dipole attractions or hydrogen bonds, while the covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong.

mcqs.q: Molecular solids are soft with low melting points because:
options: Their ionic bonds are very strong
Very little energy is needed to overcome the weak forces between their molecules, e.g. ice, solid CO2 (dry ice) and naphthalene
Each molecule is joined in a giant network
mcqs.why: Very little energy is needed to overcome the weak forces between molecules, so molecular solids are soft and possess low melting points: ice, solid CO2 (dry ice) and naphthalene are examples.

lessons.title: Crystal Lattice
lessons.notes_html:
The regular three-dimensional arrangement of particles in a crystal is described through its smallest repeating unit, the unit cell.

Unit Cell

A unit cell is the smallest portion (building block) of a crystal lattice which, when repeated over and over again in three dimensions, builds up the whole crystal. It is described by three axial distances (edge lengths) a, b and c, measured along the three axes, and three axial angles: alpha between the b and c axes, beta between the a and c axes, and gamma between the a and b axes. On the basis of these parameters, crystals are classified into seven crystal systems, such as cubic (a = b = c, all angles 90 degree) and orthorhombic (a, b and c all different in length but all angles 90 degree).

Number of Ions in the NaCl Unit Cell

In the NaCl unit cell, the Cl- ions occupy the 8 corners (8 x 1/8 = 1) and the 6 face centres (6 x 1/2 = 3), giving 4 Cl- ions. The Na+ ions occupy the 12 edges (12 x 1/4 = 3) and the body centre (1), giving 4 Na+ ions. Thus each unit cell of sodium chloride contains four Na+ and four Cl- ions, i.e. four formula units.

Lattice Energy

Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its isolated gaseous ions; it is a measure of the strength of the ionic lattice. It increases when the size of the ions decreases, because smaller ions come closer together and attract each other more strongly, e.g. LiF has a higher lattice energy than NaBr. It also increases greatly with the charge on the ions, since the electrostatic attraction is proportional to the product of the charges; thus MgO (with +2 and -2 ions) has a much higher lattice energy than NaCl (with +1 and -1 ions).

mcqs.q: A unit cell is:
options: The smallest portion (building block) of a crystal lattice which, repeated in three dimensions, builds up the whole crystal
The largest crystal that can be grown
One mole of an ionic crystal
mcqs.why: A unit cell is the smallest portion (building block) of a crystal lattice which, when repeated over and over again in three dimensions, builds up the whole crystal.

mcqs.q: The axial angles of a unit cell are defined as:
options: Alpha between a and b, beta between b and c, gamma between a and c
All three angles between a and b only
Angles measured only for cubic crystals
Alpha between b and c, beta between a and c, gamma between a and b
mcqs.why: A unit cell is described by edge lengths a, b and c and three axial angles: alpha between the b and c axes, beta between the a and c axes, and gamma between the a and b axes.

mcqs.q: A cubic crystal system has:
options: a, b and c all different, angles 90 degree
a = b = c, with all angles 90 degree
a = b, c different, one angle 120 degree
mcqs.why: In the cubic system a = b = c and all angles are 90 degree; crystals are classified into seven crystal systems on the basis of these unit-cell parameters.

mcqs.q: An orthorhombic crystal system has:
options: a = b = c, all angles 90 degree
a, b and c all different in length but all angles 90 degree
Only two edges and two angles
mcqs.why: In the orthorhombic system a, b and c are all different in length but all angles are 90 degree, one of the seven crystal systems based on unit-cell parameters.

mcqs.q: The number of Cl- ions in the NaCl unit cell is calculated as:
mcqs.why: The Cl- ions occupy the 8 corners (8 x 1/8 = 1) and the 6 face centres (6 x 1/2 = 3), giving 4 Cl- ions in the NaCl unit cell, as the working shows.

mcqs.q: The number of Na+ ions in the NaCl unit cell is calculated as:
mcqs.why: The Na+ ions occupy the 12 edges (12 x 1/4 = 3) and the body centre (1), giving 4 Na+ ions in the NaCl unit cell, as the working shows.

mcqs.q: Each unit cell of sodium chloride contains:
options: One Na+ and one Cl- ion
Six Na+ and six Cl- ions
Four Na+ and four Cl- ions, i.e. four formula units
mcqs.why: Each unit cell of sodium chloride contains four Na+ and four Cl- ions, i.e. four formula units, from the corner, face, edge and body-centre contributions.

mcqs.q: Lattice energy is defined as:
options: The energy absorbed to melt one mole of a crystal
The energy needed to break one covalent bond
The heat of sublimation of a metal
The energy released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its isolated gaseous ions
mcqs.why: Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its isolated gaseous ions; it is a measure of the strength of the ionic lattice.

mcqs.q: Lattice energy increases when ion size decreases because:
options: Ion size has no effect on lattice energy
Smaller ions come closer together and attract each other more strongly, e.g. LiF has higher lattice energy than NaBr
Smaller ions have smaller charges in every case
mcqs.why: Lattice energy increases when the size of the ions decreases, because smaller ions come closer together and attract each other more strongly; for example LiF has a higher lattice energy than NaBr.

mcqs.q: MgO has a much higher lattice energy than NaCl because:
options: Mg and O atoms are larger than Na and Cl
The electrostatic attraction is proportional to the product of the charges, and MgO has +2 and -2 ions while NaCl has +1 and -1 ions
mcqs.why: Lattice energy increases greatly with the charge on the ions, since electrostatic attraction is proportional to the product of the charges; thus MgO (with +2 and -2 ions) has a much higher lattice energy than NaCl (with +1 and -1 ions).

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.notes_html:
Many reactions do not go to completion; instead they reach a balance point called equilibrium.

Reversible Reaction

A reversible reaction is a reaction which can proceed in both the forward and the backward direction under the same conditions, and is written with a double arrow; for example, N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3. Such reactions never go to completion because the products react to reform the reactants.

Chemical Equilibrium

Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction at which the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the backward reaction. At equilibrium there is no net change in the concentrations of reactants and products with time, although both reactions continue at the microscopic level, so it is a dynamic equilibrium.

Law of Mass Action and Derivation of Kc

The law of mass action states that, at constant temperature, the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reacting species. Active mass means the molar concentration of a substance, i.e. number of moles per dm3 of solution (or partial pressure for a gas). For the general reaction aA + bB <=> cC + dD, the forward rate = kf [A]^a [B]^b and the backward rate = kb [C]^c [D]^d. At equilibrium the two rates are equal, so kf [A]^a [B]^b = kb [C]^c [D]^d. Rearranging gives kf/kb = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b) = Kc, the equilibrium constant. Its value depends only on temperature and is fixed for a given balanced equation.

Writing Kc and Kp Expressions

  • 2NO2(g) + 7H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) + 4H2O(g): Kc = [NH3]^2 [H2O]^4 / ([NO2]^2 [H2]^7), and Kp = (P NH3)^2 (P H2O)^4 / ((P NO2)^2 (P H2)^7).
  • 2H2S(g) + 3O2(g) <=> 2H2O(g) + 2SO2(g): Kc = [H2O]^2 [SO2]^2 / ([H2S]^2 [O2]^3), and Kp = (P H2O)^2 (P SO2)^2 / ((P H2S)^2 (P O2)^3).

In each expression the product concentrations are written in the numerator and the reactant concentrations in the denominator, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Kp uses partial pressures in place of concentrations for gaseous reactions. The two constants are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Dn, where Dn is the change in gas moles: for PCl5(g) <=> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), Dn = +1 so Kp > Kc, while for A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g), Dn = 0 so Kp = Kc.

Predicting Direction and Extent of Reaction from Kc

  • Direction: the reaction quotient Qc is calculated with the actual concentrations; if Qc < Kc the reaction proceeds forward, if Qc > Kc it proceeds backward, and if Qc = Kc the system is at equilibrium.
  • Extent: a large Kc (greater than 10^3) means products dominate and the reaction goes nearly to completion; a small Kc (less than 10^-3) means reactants dominate and the reaction hardly proceeds; an intermediate value means appreciable amounts of both are present.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: At 444 degree C the reaction of hydrogen and iodine is performed in a sealed 1 dm3 steel vessel: H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g). The equilibrium mixture contains 1 mole of H2, 1 mole of I2 and 7 moles of HI. Calculate (a) Kc (b) the initial concentration of H2 and I2. Solution: The vessel is 1 dm3, so moles equal molar concentrations. (a) Kc = [HI]^2/([H2][I2]) = (7)^2/(1 x 1) = 49. (b) 7 moles of HI were formed from 3.5 moles of H2 and 3.5 moles of I2, so initial H2 = 1 + 3.5 = 4.5 moles and initial I2 = 4.5 moles.

Numerical 2: In an equilibrium study of H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g) at 440 degree C, 1.2 mole of H2 and 1.2 moles of I2 were injected into an evacuated 1000 cm3 sealed flask. If Kc = 49, calculate the equilibrium concentrations. Solution: Flask volume = 1 dm3, so initial [H2] = [I2] = 1.2 mol/dm3. Let x mol/dm3 of H2 react; at equilibrium [H2] = [I2] = 1.2 - x and [HI] = 2x. Kc = (2x)^2/(1.2 - x)^2 = 49, so 2x/(1.2 - x) = 7, giving x = 0.933. Hence [H2] = [I2] = 0.267 mol/dm3 and [HI] = 1.866 mol/dm3.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction is a reaction that:
options: Goes to completion in one direction only
Occurs only in the presence of a catalyst
Can proceed in both the forward and the backward direction under the same conditions and is written with a double arrow
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction can proceed in both the forward and the backward direction under the same conditions, and is written with a double arrow, for example N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. Such reactions never go to completion because the products react to reform the reactants.

mcqs.q: Chemical equilibrium is the state at which:
options: The rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the backward reaction
All reactants have been converted to products
Concentrations of reactants and products are always equal
mcqs.why: Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction at which the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the backward reaction.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium is called dynamic because:
options: Concentrations keep changing rapidly with time
There is no net change in concentrations with time, although both reactions continue at the microscopic level
mcqs.why: At equilibrium there is no net change in the concentrations of reactants and products with time, although both reactions continue at the microscopic level, so it is a dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.q: The law of mass action states that, at constant temperature:
options: Rate depends only on the catalyst
The rate of a reaction is proportional to the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reacting species
mcqs.why: The law of mass action states that, at constant temperature, the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reacting species.

mcqs.q: Active mass means:
options: The molar concentration of a substance, i.e. number of moles per dm3 of solution (or partial pressure for a gas)
The mass in grams of a substance
The atomic mass of an element
The total volume of the vessel
mcqs.why: Active mass means the molar concentration of a substance, i.e. number of moles per dm3 of solution, or partial pressure for a gas.

mcqs.q: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant Kc is:
mcqs.why: At equilibrium kf [A]^a [B]^b = kb [C]^c [D]^d, so rearranging gives kf/kb = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b) = Kc, with products in the numerator raised to their coefficients.

mcqs.q: The value of Kc depends only on:
options: Temperature, and it is fixed for a given balanced equation

mcqs.q: For 2NO2(g) + 7H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) + 4H2O(g), Kc is:
mcqs.why: Product concentrations go in the numerator and reactant concentrations in the denominator, each raised to its coefficient, so Kc = [NH3]^2 [H2O]^4 / ([NO2]^2 [H2]^7) for this reaction.

mcqs.q: Kp differs from Kc in that Kp uses:
options: Masses in grams instead of moles
Partial pressures in place of concentrations for gaseous reactions
mcqs.why: Kp uses partial pressures in place of concentrations for gaseous reactions, while Kc uses molar concentrations; the form of the expression is otherwise the same.

mcqs.q: Kp and Kc are related by:
options: Kp = Kc(RT)^Dn, where Dn is the change in gas moles
mcqs.why: The two constants are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Dn, where Dn is the change in gas moles between products and reactants in the gaseous reaction.

options: Reactants dominate and the reaction hardly proceeds
Appreciable amounts of both reactants and products only
Kc has no relation to extent
Products dominate and the reaction goes nearly to completion
mcqs.why: A large Kc (greater than 10^3) means products dominate and the reaction goes nearly to completion; a small Kc (less than 10^-3) means reactants dominate and the reaction hardly proceeds.

mcqs.why: In a 1 dm3 vessel moles equal concentrations, so Kc = [HI]^2/([H2][I2]) = (7)^2/(1 x 1) = 49, as shown by the full working using the equilibrium amounts.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Equilibrium (Le-Chatelier's Principle)
lessons.notes_html:
A system at equilibrium responds to any disturbance by shifting so as to cancel the disturbance.

Le-Chatelier's Principle

Le-Chatelier's principle states that if a stress (change in concentration, pressure or temperature) is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that reduces the effect of the applied stress.

Effect of Pressure

A pressure increase shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas moles. The equilibrium of N2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO(g) is not affected by pressure because the number of gas moles is the same on both sides (2 = 2, Dn = 0); for this endothermic reaction only a temperature change shifts the equilibrium and changes Kc.

Effect of Catalyst

When a catalyst is added to a chemical system at equilibrium, Kc remains unchanged: a catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally and only helps equilibrium to be reached sooner.

Application: Increasing the Yield of SO3 in the Contact Process

For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g) (DH = -ve), the reaction is exothermic and shows a decrease in gas moles (3 moles give 2 moles). First, increase the pressure: the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles, producing more SO3. Second, decrease the temperature: for an exothermic reaction, lowering the temperature favours the forward direction, increasing SO3 (in practice a moderate 450 degree C is used with a V2O5 catalyst so the rate stays reasonable). Third, increase the concentration of SO2 or O2 (oxygen is used in excess), or remove SO3 as it is formed by absorbing it in concentrated H2SO4; both shift the equilibrium forward.

mcqs.q: Le-Chatelier's principle states that if a stress is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the system:
options: Shifts in the direction that increases the stress
Shifts in the direction that reduces the effect of the applied stress
mcqs.why: Le-Chatelier's principle states that if a stress (change in concentration, pressure or temperature) is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that reduces the effect of the applied stress.

mcqs.q: An increase in pressure shifts an equilibrium towards:
options: The side with more gas moles
The side with fewer gas moles
mcqs.why: A pressure increase shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas moles, because that shift reduces the effect of the increased pressure.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) is not affected by pressure because:
options: The number of gas moles is the same on both sides (2 = 2, Dn = 0)
mcqs.why: The equilibrium of N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) is not affected by pressure because the number of gas moles is the same on both sides (2 = 2, Dn = 0); for this endothermic reaction only a temperature change shifts it and changes Kc.

mcqs.q: When a catalyst is added to a system at equilibrium:
options: Kc remains unchanged; the catalyst speeds forward and backward reactions equally and equilibrium is reached sooner
Only the forward reaction speeds up
mcqs.why: When a catalyst is added, Kc remains unchanged: a catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally and only helps equilibrium to be reached sooner.

mcqs.q: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) with DH negative, the reaction is:
options: Endothermic with an increase in gas moles
Endothermic with no change in moles
Exothermic with a decrease in gas moles (3 moles give 2 moles)
Exothermic with an increase in gas moles
mcqs.why: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) (DH = -ve), the reaction is exothermic and shows a decrease in gas moles, because 3 moles of gas give 2 moles.

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure in the Contact Process:
options: Shifts equilibrium towards SO2 and O2
Changes Kc to a larger value
Shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles, producing more SO3
mcqs.why: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles, producing more SO3 in the Contact Process, by Le-Chatelier's principle.

mcqs.q: Decreasing the temperature in the Contact Process increases SO3 because:
options: For an exothermic reaction, lowering the temperature favours the forward direction
The V2O5 catalyst changes Kc at low temperature
mcqs.why: For an exothermic reaction, lowering the temperature favours the forward direction, increasing SO3; in practice a moderate 450 degree C is used with a V2O5 catalyst so the rate stays reasonable.

mcqs.q: The practical conditions used to keep a reasonable rate in the Contact Process are:
options: 0 degree C with an iron catalyst
450 degree C with a V2O5 catalyst
Room temperature with concentrated H2SO4 as catalyst
mcqs.why: In practice a moderate 450 degree C is used with a V2O5 catalyst so the rate stays reasonable, even though a lower temperature would favour the exothermic forward reaction.

mcqs.q: Increasing the concentration of SO2 or using oxygen in excess in the Contact Process:
options: Shifts the equilibrium forward, producing more SO3
Removes the need for a catalyst by changing Kc
mcqs.why: Increasing the concentration of SO2 or O2 (oxygen is used in excess) shifts the equilibrium forward, producing more SO3, by Le-Chatelier's principle.

mcqs.q: SO3 is removed as it is formed in the Contact Process by:
options: Absorbing it in concentrated H2SO4, which shifts the equilibrium forward
Adding water to the equilibrium mixture
mcqs.why: Removing SO3 as it is formed, by absorbing it in concentrated H2SO4, shifts the equilibrium forward and increases the yield of SO3.

lessons.title: Industrial Application of Le-Chatelier's Principle (Haber's Process)
lessons.notes_html:
The manufacture of ammonia is the classic industrial application of Le-Chatelier's principle.

The Haber Process Equilibrium

N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, DH = -92 KJ/mol. There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, and the reaction is exothermic.

Choosing the Industrial Conditions

  • Pressure: a high pressure (about 200 atm) shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia, the side with fewer gas moles.
  • Temperature: a lower temperature favours ammonia because the reaction is exothermic, but would make the rate too slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 degree C is used.
  • Catalyst: an iron catalyst speeds up the attainment of equilibrium without changing Kc.
  • Removal of product: ammonia is condensed and removed so the equilibrium keeps shifting forward.

mcqs.q: The Haber Process equilibrium, with its enthalpy change, is:
mcqs.why: The Haber Process equilibrium is N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, DH = -92 KJ/mol; the reaction is exothermic, with 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right.

mcqs.q: In the Haber equilibrium, the gas moles change from:
options: 4 moles on the left to 2 on the right
2 moles on the left to 4 on the right
mcqs.why: There are 4 moles of gas on the left (1 N2 + 3 H2) and 2 moles of NH3 on the right, so increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.

mcqs.q: A high pressure of about 200 atm is used in the Haber Process because it:
options: Shifts the equilibrium towards nitrogen and hydrogen
Changes Kc to a bigger value
Makes the iron catalyst work as a reactant
Shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia, the side with fewer gas moles
mcqs.why: A high pressure (about 200 atm) shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia, the side with fewer gas moles, increasing the yield by Le-Chatelier's principle.

mcqs.q: A lower temperature favours ammonia in the Haber Process because:
options: The reaction is exothermic, so lowering temperature favours the forward direction
Low temperature increases Kc for every reaction equally
Ammonia condenses only below 0 degree C
mcqs.why: A lower temperature favours ammonia because the forward reaction is exothermic (DH = -92 KJ/mol), so cooling shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction.

mcqs.q: Why is a compromise temperature of about 450 degree C used in the Haber Process?
options: It is the melting point of iron
A lower temperature would favour ammonia but would make the rate too slow, so 450 degree C balances yield and rate
A higher temperature gives more ammonia
450 degree C changes Kc to its maximum
mcqs.why: A lower temperature favours ammonia but would make the rate too slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 degree C is used to keep a reasonable rate.

mcqs.q: The catalyst used in the Haber Process, and its effect, is:
options: Iron; it speeds up attainment of equilibrium without changing Kc
mcqs.why: An iron catalyst speeds up the attainment of equilibrium without changing Kc; it speeds the forward and backward reactions equally.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is condensed and removed during the Haber Process so that:
options: The equilibrium keeps shifting forward to replace the removed ammonia
mcqs.why: Ammonia is condensed and removed so the equilibrium keeps shifting forward, by Le-Chatelier's principle, to produce more ammonia.

mcqs.q: Which set of conditions belongs to the Haber Process as described in the lesson?
options: About 200 atm, 1000 degree C, no catalyst
About 200 atm, about 450 degree C, iron catalyst, ammonia condensed and removed
Low pressure, low temperature, no removal of ammonia
mcqs.why: The Haber conditions are high pressure about 200 atm, compromise temperature about 450 degree C, an iron catalyst, and removal of ammonia by condensation, all chosen using Le-Chatelier's principle.

mcqs.q: Increasing pressure alone in the Haber Process does NOT:
options: Shift equilibrium towards fewer gas moles
Increase the proportion of ammonia at equilibrium
mcqs.why: Pressure shifts the position of equilibrium towards ammonia but does not change Kc; Kc depends only on temperature, so a pressure change leaves Kc unchanged.

mcqs.q: The Haber Process is an industrial application of:
mcqs.why: The manufacture of ammonia is the classic industrial application of Le-Chatelier's principle, with pressure, temperature, catalyst and product removal chosen to maximise ammonia.

lessons.title: Solubility Product
lessons.notes_html:
Sparingly soluble salts dissolve only to a very small extent, and their saturated solutions are described by a special equilibrium constant, Ksp.

Solubility Product (Ksp)

The solubility product (Ksp) is the product of the molar concentrations of the ions of a sparingly soluble salt in its saturated solution at a given temperature, each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the dissociation equation.

Ksp Expressions

  • BaF2 <=> Ba2+ + 2F-: Ksp = [Ba2+][F-]^2
  • Li2C2O4 <=> 2Li+ + C2O4 2-: Ksp = [Li+]^2 [C2O4 2-]
  • MgCO3 <=> Mg2+ + CO3 2-: Ksp = [Mg2+][CO3 2-]
  • Ag3PO4 <=> 3Ag+ + PO4 3-: Ksp = [Ag+]^3 [PO4 3-]

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: Lead fluoride (PbF2) is used in glass coating to reflect IR rays. Its solubility in water at 25 degree C is 0.58 g/dm3. Calculate its Ksp (atomic mass of Pb = 207 and F = 19). Solution: Molar mass of PbF2 = 207 + 2(19) = 245 g/mol. Molar solubility s = 0.58/245 = 2.37 x 10^-3 mol/dm3. PbF2 <=> Pb2+ + 2F-, so [Pb2+] = s and [F-] = 2s. Ksp = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3 = 4 x (2.37 x 10^-3)^3 = 5.3 x 10^-8 mol3/dm9.

Numerical 2: A solution is prepared by mixing 200 cm3 of 2.4 x 10^-4M Ca(NO3)2 and 300 cm3 of 4.5 x 10^-2M K2CO3. Will CaCO3 precipitate on cooling to 25 degree C if Ksp of CaCO3 at 25 degree C is 3.8 x 10^-9? Solution: Total volume = 500 cm3. After mixing, [Ca2+] = 2.4 x 10^-4 x (200/500) = 9.6 x 10^-5 M, and [CO3 2-] = 4.5 x 10^-2 x (300/500) = 2.7 x 10^-2 M. Ionic product Qsp = 9.6 x 10^-5 x 2.7 x 10^-2 = 2.6 x 10^-6. Since Qsp is greater than Ksp (3.8 x 10^-9), the solution is supersaturated and CaCO3 will precipitate.

lessons.title: Common Ion Effect
lessons.notes_html:
Adding an ion that is already present in an equilibrium suppresses the dissolution or ionization of the electrolyte.

What is the Common Ion Effect?

The common ion effect is the decrease in the solubility (or ionization) of a sparingly soluble salt or weak electrolyte when a highly soluble electrolyte containing an ion common to it is added to its solution. It is an application of Le-Chatelier's principle.

Examples

  • The solubility of AgCl decreases when NaCl is added, because the extra Cl- ions shift the equilibrium AgCl(s) <=> Ag+ + Cl- to the left and more AgCl precipitates.
  • NH4Cl suppresses the ionization of weak NH4OH by supplying NH4+ ions.

Applications

  • Qualitative analysis of salts.
  • Salting out of soaps.
  • Purification of salts.

lessons.title: Acidic, Basic and Amphoteric Substances
lessons.notes_html:
Oxides and other substances are classified as acidic, basic or amphoteric according to how they react with acids and bases.

Types of Oxides

  • Acidic oxides react with bases, e.g. CO2.
  • Basic oxides react with acids, e.g. K2O and CaO.
  • Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases to form salt and water.

Amphoteric Behaviour of Al2O3

Al2O3 is an amphoteric oxide because it reacts with both acids and base: with HCl it behaves as a base and with NaOH it behaves as an acid, forming salt and water in each case. This dual behaviour is the test of an amphoteric substance.

Identifying Properties of Bases

  • Bases have bitter tastes.
  • They have high pH values.
  • They react with acids to form salts.
  • They turn red litmus blue (acids turn blue litmus red).

lessons.title: The Bronsted-Lowry Theory of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
The Bronsted-Lowry theory defines acids and bases in terms of proton transfer, so it applies beyond aqueous solutions.

Definitions

  • An acid is a species which tends to donate a proton (H+).
  • A base is a species which tends to accept a proton.

Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs

When an acid donates a proton, the species left behind can accept a proton back and is called its conjugate base; similarly, a base accepting a proton becomes its conjugate acid. A conjugate acid-base pair is two species that differ by only one proton, one on each side of the equation. For example, in HCl + H2O <=> H3O+ + Cl-, HCl/Cl- and H3O+/H2O are conjugate pairs. Water can act as an acid with NH3 and as a base with HCl, so it is amphoteric in this theory.

lessons.title: Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
lessons.notes_html:
Every acid has its own conjugate base, and every base its own conjugate acid; members of a pair differ by exactly one proton (H+), e.g. NH4+ and NH3.

Conjugate Bases of Given Acids

A conjugate base is formed when an acid loses one proton:

  • H2SO4 -> HSO4- (bisulphate ion)
  • H2S -> HS- (bisulphide ion)
  • NH4+ -> NH3 (ammonia)
  • HCOOH -> HCOO- (formate ion)

In each pair the acid and its conjugate base differ by exactly one proton, and a strong acid has a weak conjugate base. The conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+, formed by gaining a proton.

Identifying Conjugate Pairs in Reactions

  • Acetic acid and ammonia: CH3COOH + NH3 <=> CH3COO- + NH4+. CH3COOH (acid) and CH3COO- (its conjugate base) form one pair, and NH4+ (conjugate acid) and NH3 (base) form the other pair; the proton passes from acetic acid to ammonia.
  • Hydrochloric acid and water: HCl + H2O <=> Cl- + H3O+. HCl (acid) and Cl- (its conjugate base) form one pair, and H3O+ (conjugate acid) and H2O (base) form the other pair.

mcqs.why: H2S loses one proton to give HS-, the bisulphide ion, which is its conjugate base.

mcqs.why: NH4+ -> NH3 on losing a proton, so ammonia is the conjugate base of the ammonium ion.

mcqs.why: HCOOH loses one proton to form HCOO-, the formate ion, its conjugate base.

mcqs.why: The conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+, formed when ammonia gains one proton.

lessons.title: Strengths of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
The strength of an acid or base depends on how completely it ionizes in water, and the pH scale measures the resulting acidity.

Strong and Weak Acids

Acid strength depends on the extent of ionization: H2SO4 is a stronger acid than CH3COOH because its degree of ionization is high — it ionizes almost completely in water — while CH3COOH ionizes only slightly. A strong acid has a weak conjugate base, and a weak acid has a strong conjugate base.

Self-Ionization of Water and Kw

Self-ionization of water is the process in which one water molecule donates a proton to another water molecule, producing hydronium and hydroxide ions: 2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-. The ionic product of water is expressed as Kw = [H+][OH-] (more exactly [H3O+][OH-]). Its value at 25 degree C is 1 x 10^-14 mol2/dm6. In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7 M, which is why pure water is neutral with pH 7 at this temperature.

pH and pOH

  • pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, pH = -log[H+]; it measures the acidity of a solution on a scale from 0 to 14.
  • pOH is the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration, pOH = -log[OH-].
  • From Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degree C, taking the negative log of both sides gives pH + pOH = 14.
  • A solution with pH less than 7 is acidic, equal to 7 neutral, and greater than 7 basic.

Worked Numericals

Numerical 1: A solution is made by dissolving 14.8g HCl in water at 25 degree C. If the volume of solution is 750 cm3 and HCl is assumed to be completely ionized, calculate its pH. Solution: Moles of HCl = 14.8/36.5 = 0.405 mol in 0.750 dm3, so [H+] = 0.405/0.750 = 0.54 mol/dm3. pH = -log(0.54) = 0.27. (Working with the given data gives pH about 0.27; the book prints the answer as pH = 1.2, which corresponds to about one-tenth of this concentration.)

Numerical 2: The hydroxide ion concentration in an antiseptic solution at 25 degree C is 3.5 x 10^-4M. Calculate its pH. Solution: pOH = -log(3.5 x 10^-4) = 4 - log 3.5 = 4 - 0.54 = 3.46. Using pH + pOH = 14, pH = 14 - 3.46 = 10.54, so the solution is basic. (The book prints the answer as pH = 8; the value calculated from the given hydroxide ion concentration is about 10.5.)

lessons.title: Lewis Definition of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
The Lewis theory is the most general theory of acids and bases because it is based on electron pairs rather than protons.

Lewis Definitions

  • A Lewis acid is a substance that can accept an electron pair.
  • A Lewis base is a substance that can donate an electron pair.

Thus BF3 is a Lewis acid because boron has an incomplete octet and accepts a lone pair from NH3, which is a Lewis base; the product is a coordinate (adduct) compound.

Advantages over the Bronsted-Lowry Theory

  • It is not limited to proton transfer or to aqueous solutions, so reactions like BF3 + NH3 and metal ion complex formation are included as acid-base reactions.
  • It explains the acidic behaviour of oxides such as CO2 and SO3 and of metal ions.
  • Hence it is the most general theory of acids and bases.

lessons.title: Buffer Solutions and their Applications
lessons.notes_html:
A buffer solution keeps its pH almost constant when small amounts of acid or base are added to it.

What is a Buffer Solution?

A buffer solution is a mixture of a weak acid with its salt of a strong base (acidic buffer), or a weak base with its salt of a strong acid (basic buffer), which resists a change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added. Examples are CH3COOH/CH3COONa, Na2CO3/NaHCO3 and NH4OH/NH4Cl. NaOH/HCl is not a buffer because it is a mixture of a strong base and a strong acid, not a weak acid/base with its salt.

How a Buffer Resists Change of pH

In an acidic buffer like CH3COOH/CH3COONa, added H+ ions are removed by the acetate ions to form weakly ionized acetic acid, and added OH- ions are removed by the acetic acid to form acetate and water, so the pH stays nearly constant. The range over which a buffer is effective is called its buffer range.

Applications of Buffer Solutions

  • Maintaining the pH of blood (about 7.4).
  • Fermentation and dyeing industries.
  • Chemical analysis.
  • Medicines and shampoos.

lessons.title: Salts, their Types and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Salts are the products of neutralization, and their behaviour in water depends on the strength of the parent acid and base.

What is a Salt?

A salt is an ionic compound formed by the neutralization reaction of an acid and a base, in which the H+ of the acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion, e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.

Types of Salts

  • Acidic salts still contain replaceable hydrogen and are formed by partial neutralization of a polybasic acid, e.g. NaHSO4 and NaHCO3.
  • Basic salts still contain an OH group and are formed by partial neutralization of a polyacidic base, e.g. Mg(OH)Cl.
  • Neutral (normal) salts are formed by complete neutralization and contain neither replaceable H nor OH, e.g. NaCl, Na2SO4 and CaCO3.

Hydrolysis of Salts

Hydrolysis is the reaction of the cation or anion of a salt with water, which changes the pH of the solution.

  • K2CO3 (strong base + weak acid): the CO3 2- ion hydrolyzes to produce OH- ions, so the solution is alkaline (pH > 7). Similarly Na2CO3 solution is alkaline because CO3 2- + H2O -> HCO3- + OH-.
  • (NH4)2SO4 (weak base + strong acid): the NH4+ ion hydrolyzes to produce H+ ions, so the solution is acidic (pH < 7). Similarly NH4Cl solution is acidic because NH4+ + H2O -> NH4OH + H+.
  • NaNO3 (strong base + strong acid): neither Na+ nor NO3- hydrolyzes appreciably, so the solution remains neutral (pH = 7). NaCl likewise does not hydrolyze and does not alter the pH of a solution.
  • Na2CO3 is the salt formed by neutralization of a weak acid (H2CO3) and a strong base (NaOH), and NH4CN is the salt of a weak acid (HCN) and a weak base (NH4OH).

In general, cation hydrolysis gives an acidic solution and anion hydrolysis gives a basic solution.

mcqs.why: In salt formation, for example HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O, H+ is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.

mcqs.why: Basic salts still contain an OH group, for example Mg(OH)Cl, from partial neutralization of a polyacidic base.

mcqs.why: Neutral salts contain neither replaceable hydrogen nor an OH group because neutralization is complete.

mcqs.why: CO3 2- + H2O -> HCO3- + OH-, so carbonate salts of a strong base and weak acid give alkaline solutions.

options: NH4+ hydrolyzes to produce H+ ions
mcqs.why: NH4+ + H2O -> NH4OH + H+, so salts of a weak base and strong acid give acidic solutions by cation hydrolysis.

mcqs.why: NaNO3 is from a strong base and strong acid; neither ion hydrolyzes appreciably, so the solution stays neutral.

mcqs.why: Cation hydrolysis produces H+ and an acidic solution, while anion hydrolysis produces OH- and a basic solution.

lessons.title: Chemical Kinetics
lessons.notes_html:
Chemical kinetics is the study of the rates of chemical reactions and the factors that affect them. Some reactions are fast, some moderate and some slow: ionic reactions, which involve only the combination of ions already present in solution and need almost no bond breaking, are fast (instantaneous) reactions.

Rate of Reaction

Rate of reaction is the decrease in concentration of a reactant or the increase in concentration of a product per unit time during a chemical reaction. For A -> B, the rate of disappearance of A is written -dA/dt (with a negative sign because the concentration of A decreases, so that the rate is a positive quantity) and the rate of appearance of B is +dB/dt.

Velocity of Reaction

Velocity of reaction is the rate at a particular instant (instantaneous rate), measured from the slope of a concentration-time graph at that point. The best alternative term for the velocity of reaction is the instantaneous rate.

Order of Reaction

Order of reaction is the sum of the powers to which the concentrations of the reactants are raised in the experimental rate law; it may be a whole number, a fraction or even zero. R = K means the rate does not depend on any concentration, so the reaction is of zero order.

Rate Constant

The rate constant (specific rate constant) is the rate of reaction when the molar concentration of each reactant is unity; its value depends only on temperature (and a catalyst), not on concentration or time.

Rate of ReactionRate Constant
Change in concentration per unit timeRate when each concentration is unity
Changes as the reaction proceedsStays constant at a fixed temperature

Elementary and Overall Reactions

An elementary reaction takes place in a single step, while an overall reaction is the sum of several elementary steps (its mechanism).

mcqs.why: Ionic reactions involve ions already present in solution and need almost no bond breaking, so they are fast.

mcqs.why: The lesson states that the best alternative term for velocity of reaction is the instantaneous rate.

mcqs.why: Order is the sum of the powers of concentrations in the experimental rate law; it may be whole, fractional or zero.

mcqs.why: R = K means rate is independent of concentration, which is the definition of a zero order reaction.

mcqs.why: The rate constant is the rate when the molar concentration of each reactant is unity.
